R.q:
At a town meeting, the director of the Hillside Community Clinic said, "Our budget is $40,000 short this year. Either we close the clinic on Saturdays, or we raise the fee for every visit by $20. There is no other way to balance the books." Several residents pointed out that the clinic had not yet applied for a state grant, asked local businesses for support, or reviewed its supply costs.

Which fallacy does the director's statement contain?
o: Straw man
Slippery slope
Red herring
False dilemma
R.w: The director presents two options as the only choices, while residents name several others (a grant, business support, lower supply costs). Ignoring other options is a false dilemma.

n.0: A straw man misrepresents an opponent's position; the director does not describe anyone else's view.
n.1: A slippery slope predicts a chain of worsening events; the director predicts no chain.
n.2: A red herring switches to an unrelated topic; the director stays on the budget.

R.q:
Ridgeline Hospital's emergency department has grown busier. In 2019 it recorded about 41,000 visits; last year it recorded about 52,000. Hospital leaders say they will add eight treatment rooms and hire more nurses by next summer.
Emergency visits by time of arrival, last year
7 a.m. to 3 p.m. | 38%
3 p.m. to 11 p.m. | 45%
11 p.m. to 7 a.m. | 17%

What information does the table provide that the passage does not?
o: Which part of the day brings the largest share of emergency visits
Why most patients chose to come to the emergency department
How many treatment rooms the hospital plans to add next summer
How much the total number of yearly visits has grown since 2019
R.w: The table breaks last year's visits down by time of arrival, showing that 3 p.m. to 11 p.m. has the largest share (45 percent). The passage gives only yearly totals and plans.

n.1: Neither source gives reasons for visits; the table shows only arrival times.
n.2: The eight new rooms are mentioned in the passage, not the table.
n.3: The growth from about 41,000 to about 52,000 visits comes from the passage.

R.q:
Passage 1
A 2023 study of six middle schools found that students threw away about a third of the food on their lunch trays. Fruit and vegetables were discarded most often. The waste costs districts money and sends tons of food to landfills each year.

Passage 2
This fall, Riverside Middle School placed a share table near the cafeteria exit. Students leave unopened milk, packaged snacks, and whole fruit they do not want, and classmates may take them. A local food pantry collects what is left each Friday. Food waste in the cafeteria fell by about 30 percent in three months.

Which statement best describes how Passage 2 relates to Passage 1?
o: It questions the data that Passage 1 uses to describe cafeteria waste.
It narrows Passage 1's topic to the cost of school lunches.
It repeats the main claim of Passage 1 using new statistics.
It describes one approach to the problem that Passage 1 explains.
R.w: Passage 1 describes the problem of cafeteria food waste. Passage 2 reports one school's share table and the 30 percent drop in waste that followed, which is a response to that problem.

n.0: Passage 2 never disputes Passage 1's findings; it assumes waste is a problem worth reducing.
n.1: Passage 2 does not discuss lunch costs; it describes a program that reduces waste.
n.2: Passage 2's statistic measures the result of a solution, not the size of the problem.

R.q:
From a clinic manager's memo: Starting next month, I recommend that we ask every patient with high blood pressure to use the PulseTrack phone app to log their readings. My neighbor started using PulseTrack in March. She checks her pressure every morning, and her readings are the best they have been in years. The app is free and easy to set up, so there is no reason to wait.

Which statement best evaluates the evidence in the memo?
o: It is strong, because the neighbor's readings improved after she began using the app.
It is irrelevant, because a phone app has no connection to blood pressure readings.
It is insufficient, because one person's results cannot show the app helps most patients.
It is credible, because the manager watched the neighbor's results firsthand each day.
R.w: The only evidence is one neighbor's experience. It is relevant, but a single anecdote is not enough to show that the app would help a clinic's whole patient population.

n.0: Improvement after starting the app is one case and may have other causes; it does not make the evidence strong.
n.1: The app logs blood pressure readings, so the evidence is related to the claim; the problem is its amount.
n.3: The memo does not say the manager observed daily results, and even firsthand observation of one person is too little evidence.

R.q:
A Nutrition Facts label lists the serving size at the top, followed by the number of calories in one serving. Below that, the label shows nutrients such as fat, sodium and added sugars, along with a Percent Daily Value for each. A Percent Daily Value of 5 percent or less means a food is low in that nutrient, and 20 percent or more means it is high. All of these numbers apply to one serving, so a person who eats two servings must double them.

Which sentence, if added to the end of the passage, would best fit the author's purpose?
o: Percent Daily Values are based on a 2,000-calorie diet for a typical adult.
Food companies make labels confusing so that shoppers will buy more.
I still remember how confused I was the first time I tried to read a label.
Every family should stop buying snacks with more than 10 grams of added sugar.
R.w: The passage explains, in a neutral way, how to read the parts of a label, so its purpose is to inform. A sentence adding another factual detail about the label (the 2,000-calorie basis of Percent Daily Values) continues that purpose.

n.1: This accuses companies of a motive without evidence, adding a biased claim that does not match the neutral explanation.
n.2: A personal memory would add an expressive, first-person note to an impersonal explanation.
n.3: This tells families what they should do, which would shift the passage from informing to persuading.

R.q:
Every high school graduate in our state should leave knowing how to perform CPR. When a person's heart stops outside a hospital, the chance of survival drops with each minute before chest compressions begin, and many of these emergencies happen at home, in front of family members. Critics say schools already have too little time for core subjects. Yet hands-only CPR can be taught in a single 30-minute session, often during an existing health class. Several states already require the lesson, and none has reported that it crowded out other learning.

The sentence "Critics say schools already have too little time for core subjects" mainly serves to
o: concede that the author's proposal should wait until a later year
present an opposing view that the author then goes on to answer
give evidence that CPR training improves survival after cardiac arrest
state the main claim that the author supports throughout the passage
R.w: The sentence reports what critics say, and the next sentence begins "Yet" and answers it (the lesson takes one 30-minute session). It introduces a counterclaim that the author rebuts.

n.0: The author does not concede the point; the next sentence rejects it.
n.2: The survival evidence is in the second sentence; this sentence is about class time.
n.3: The main claim is the first sentence: every graduate should know CPR. This sentence presents a view that challenges it.

R.q:
Letter to the editor: Nearly everyone I know in Maple Heights has already signed the petition against the new cell tower on Birch Road, so the council should listen to the community and reject it. Think about your children sleeping a few hundred feet from that tower every single night. Do you really want to gamble with their health? Vote no before it is too late.

Which fallacies does the letter contain? Select all that apply.
o: Ad hominem
Straw man
Bandwagon
Appeal to false authority
Circular reasoning
Appeal to fear
R.w: "Nearly everyone I know has signed" argues from popularity (bandwagon). The image of children sleeping near the tower and "gamble with their health" try to frighten readers without any evidence of harm (appeal to fear).

n.0: The letter does not attack any person who supports the tower.
n.1: The letter never states or distorts an opponent's position.
n.3: No expert or celebrity is cited.
n.4: The letter's reasons (the petition, fear for children) are separate from its conclusion, even though they are weak.

R.q:
Read the memo.

To: All Third-Floor Staff
From: Janet Liu, Nurse Manager
Date: March 3
Subject: Supply room

Starting Monday, the third-floor supply room will be locked at all times, and staff will badge in to enter. Each item removed must be scanned at the new station by the door. Please do not prop the door open, even during busy shifts. Last month's inventory showed that we were billed for far more wound-care supplies than were charted for patients. Thank you for helping us keep costs under control.

Which of the following can most reasonably be inferred from the memo?
o: The manager believes supplies have been leaving the room without being recorded.
The supply room was previously locked during night shifts but not day shifts.
The hospital plans to stop stocking wound-care supplies on the third floor.
Staff members have been taking wound-care supplies home for their own use.
R.w: The memo pairs new controls (locking, badging, scanning each item) with a gap between supplies billed and supplies charted. The most reasonable inference is that the manager thinks items are being removed without a record.

n.1: Unsupported: the memo says nothing about the room's earlier locking schedule.
n.2: Unsupported: the memo changes how supplies are accessed, not whether they are stocked.
n.3: Overreaches: unrecorded use could come from charting errors or waste; the memo never accuses anyone of taking supplies home.

R.q:
Last week, the board of directors of Northfield Health announced a scheme to swallow up beloved St. Anne's Hospital. Under the merger, St. Anne's would keep its emergency department but close its maternity ward, and expectant mothers would travel 25 miles to Northfield's main campus. The board says the change will save $4 million a year. A public hearing is scheduled for March 12 at the county courthouse.

Which of the following words or phrases from the passage are examples of loaded language? Select all that apply.
o: swallow up
announced
scheme
merger
beloved
board of directors
R.w: "Scheme" suggests a sneaky plot, "swallow up" suggests a greedy takeover, and "beloved" adds warm emotion to one side. Each word carries a strong connotation that pushes the reader toward the author's view, which is what loaded language does.

n.1: "Announced" is a neutral verb for making information public.
n.3: "Merger" is the standard, neutral business term for two organizations combining.
n.5: "Board of directors" is the neutral name for the group that governs the company.

R.q:
Read the passage.

Tetanus: What You Should Know
What is tetanus? Tetanus is a serious illness caused by bacteria whose spores live in soil, dust and animal manure. It is not spread from person to person.
How do people get it? The spores enter the body through breaks in the skin, most often deep puncture wounds such as those from stepping on a nail.
What are the symptoms? The most common first sign is cramping of the jaw muscles, which is why tetanus is sometimes called lockjaw. Painful muscle stiffness can then spread through the body.
How can I prevent it? Adults need a tetanus booster every 10 years. If you get a deep or dirty wound and your last booster was more than 5 years ago, a doctor may recommend a booster right away.

According to the passage, when might a doctor recommend a tetanus booster sooner than the usual 10 years?
o: When a person with a dirty wound had a booster over 5 years ago
When a person has spent time with someone who has tetanus
When a person regularly works with soil, dust or animal manure
When a person begins to feel cramping in the muscles of the jaw
R.w: Under "How can I prevent it?" the passage says that after a deep or dirty wound, a doctor may recommend a booster right away if the last one was more than 5 years ago.

n.1: Contradicted: the passage says tetanus is not spread from person to person.
n.2: Soil, dust and manure are where spores live; the passage does not link working with them to an early booster.
n.3: Jaw cramping is listed under symptoms as a first sign of the illness, not as a reason for an early booster.

R.q:
The HomeCheck 300 blood pressure monitor takes a reading in about 40 seconds and stores up to 120 results for two users. It runs on four AA batteries or the included wall adapter. The large, backlit screen is easy to read, and the cuff fits upper arms from 9 to 17 inches around. HomeCheck monitors have been sold in pharmacies since 2016. At $49.99, the HomeCheck 300 is a bargain, and customers will love how simple it is to use.

Which of the following statements from the product description are opinions? Select all that apply.
o: Customers will love how simple it is to use.
It runs on four AA batteries or the included wall adapter.
The cuff fits upper arms from 9 to 17 inches around.
HomeCheck monitors have been sold in pharmacies since 2016.
At $49.99, the HomeCheck 300 is a bargain.
The large, backlit screen is easy to read.
R.w: "Easy to read," "a bargain" and "customers will love" are judgments or predictions about feelings that buyers could dispute. The screen being large and backlit and the price being $49.99 are checkable, but each sentence's main claim is a judgment, so all three are opinions.

n.1: The power options can be checked by examining the product, so this is a fact.
n.2: The cuff range is a measurement that can be confirmed, so this is a fact.
n.3: Sales history can be confirmed through company or pharmacy records, so this is a fact.

R.q:
When Jasmine opened the supply closet at the start of her shift, she found it in disarray. Rolls of gauze, boxes of gloves and packets of syringes were jumbled together on the same shelves, and nothing was where the labels said it would be. Every item on her restocking checklist was there, but it took her twenty minutes to sort everything back into place.

As used in the passage, the word disarray most nearly means
o: a shortage of supplies.
a state of disrepair.
a state of disorder.
an unsanitary condition.
R.w: "Jumbled together," "nothing was where the labels said" and the need to "sort everything back into place" all describe a mess. Disarray means disorder.

n.0: Every item on her checklist was there; the problem was where the supplies were, not how many there were.
n.1: "Disrepair" looks similar, but it means broken or damaged. Nothing in the closet is described as broken, and Jasmine fixes the problem by sorting, not repairing.
n.3: Nothing mentions dirt or contamination; the items are mixed up, not unclean.

R.q:
Read the sentences from a short story set in a pediatric clinic.

Her laugh rang out like a bell across the waiting room. By noon, the waiting room was an oven. The toddler was as restless as a puppy in a bathtub. Parents who would like a blanket for their child can ask at the desk. The old radiator groaned and complained all morning. The receptionist moved through the crowd like a seasoned conductor.

Which of the following sentences contain a simile? Select all that apply.
o: The toddler was as restless as a puppy in a bathtub.
Parents who would like a blanket for their child can ask at the desk.
The old radiator groaned and complained all morning.
By noon, the waiting room was an oven.
Her laugh rang out like a bell across the waiting room.
The receptionist moved through the crowd like a seasoned conductor.
R.w: A simile compares two unlike things using "like" or "as." The laugh is compared to a bell, the toddler to a puppy, and the receptionist to a conductor.

n.1: "Would like" means "want"; the word "like" here makes no comparison.
n.2: Groaning and complaining are human actions given to a radiator, which is personification.
n.3: This compares the room to an oven directly, without "like" or "as," so it is a metaphor.

R.q:
At a public meeting, several residents asked the hospital's spokesperson why parking fees in the visitor garage had doubled this year. The spokesperson replied, "I understand your concern. But let me tell you about our new rooftop garden, which gives patients a peaceful place to recover. It was funded by donors and has been praised by patients and their families." She then invited the next question, and the parking fees were not discussed again.

Which fallacy does the spokesperson's reply contain?
o: Red herring
Ad hominem
Straw man
Bandwagon
R.w: The question was about parking fees, and the spokesperson shifts attention to the rooftop garden, a topic unrelated to the fees. Distracting from the issue with an irrelevant topic is a red herring.

n.1: The spokesperson does not attack the residents who asked the question.
n.2: A straw man restates the opponent's view in a distorted form; the spokesperson does not restate the residents' concern at all.
n.3: The reply mentions praise for the garden but does not argue that fees are fair because many people agree.

R.q:
Passage 1
From a second-grade teacher: Studies of young children find little link between nightly homework and better grades. Worksheets often lead to tears at the kitchen table. I now ask families for one thing: read together for twenty minutes each night.

Passage 2
From a parent: My daughter's weekly homework packet does more than review math facts. It teaches her to manage her time and finish a task without being told twice. It also shows me what she is learning, so I can help when she struggles. I hope the school keeps assigning it.

The authors disagree most about whether
o: homework improves the grades of older students
reading at home each night benefits young children
young children should be given regular homework
parents should know what children learn at school
R.w: The teacher has replaced homework with shared reading because of weak evidence, while the parent wants the school to keep the weekly packet. Their conflict is over assigning homework to young children.

n.0: Both passages concern young children; neither discusses older students.
n.1: The teacher recommends nightly reading, and the parent never questions it, so this is not a point of disagreement.
n.3: The parent values knowing what her child learns; the teacher does not argue against it.

R.q:
Each winter, clinic phones ring with requests for antibiotics to treat colds. Many callers believe the drugs will help them get over a cold sooner. Colds, however, are caused by viruses, and antibiotics work against bacteria, not viruses. Taking antibiotics when they are not needed can cause side effects such as diarrhea and rashes, and it helps bacteria become resistant to the drugs. Rest, fluids and time remain the main treatment for most colds.

Which misconception does the passage seek to correct?
o: That antibiotics will help a person recover from a cold faster
That colds are caused by viruses rather than by bacteria
That antibiotics can cause side effects such as diarrhea and rashes
That rest and fluids are the main treatment for most colds
R.w: The passage reports the belief that antibiotics shorten a cold and then explains why it is wrong: antibiotics act on bacteria, and colds are viral. A commonly held but incorrect belief is a misconception.

n.1: This is the correct information the author uses to correct the misconception, not the misconception itself.
n.2: The author states this as a fact to show why unneeded antibiotics are harmful.
n.3: The author endorses this as the accurate treatment advice; it is not presented as a mistaken belief.

R.q:
Read the excerpt from the index of a health textbook.

Diabetes, 112-131
   gestational, 127-128
   insipidus, 129-130
   type 1, 114-118
   type 2, 119-126
      diet and, 122-123
      exercise and, 124
Diabetic ketoacidosis, 117
Diabetic retinopathy, 125, 302
Diagnosis (see also Laboratory tests)
   of anemia, 88
   of diabetes, 116, 120
   of hypertension, 70-71
Dialysis, 204-207
Diaphragm, 140-141
Diarrhea, 188-190
Diet
   heart-healthy, 64-66
   for kidney disease, 208
   low-sodium, 72
Digestion, 176-199
   enzymes in, 181-183
   role of the liver in, 190-192
Digital thermometer, use of, 12

A student wants to read about how type 2 diabetes is diagnosed. Based on the index, which page is most likely to have this information?
o: Page 120
Page 88
Page 124
Page 116
R.w: Diagnosis of diabetes appears on pages 116 and 120. Type 2 diabetes covers pages 119-126, so page 120 is the diagnosis page that falls inside the type 2 section.

n.1: Page 88 covers the diagnosis of anemia, a different condition under the same heading.
n.2: Page 124 covers exercise and type 2 diabetes, not diagnosis.
n.3: Page 116 discusses diagnosing diabetes, but it falls in the type 1 range (114-118).

R.q:
Read the instructions.

Home Blood Pressure Log: Instructions from Dr. Kim's Office
Sit quietly for 5 minutes before measuring, with your feet flat and your arm resting at heart level. Take two readings, one minute apart, and record both.
If either top number is 180 or higher, wait 5 minutes and measure again. If it is still 180 or higher, call 911 if you have chest pain, shortness of breath or trouble speaking; otherwise, call our office right away.
If both top numbers are between 140 and 179, record them and bring the log to your next visit.
If both top numbers are below 140, record them as usual.

Mr. Adeyemi's two readings have top numbers of 184 and 176. Five minutes later, his top number is 182. He has no chest pain, shortness of breath or trouble speaking.

According to the instructions, what should Mr. Adeyemi do?
o: Call Dr. Kim's office right away
Wait another 5 minutes and take two more readings
Record the readings and bring the log to his next visit
Call 911, because one of his readings was 180 or higher
R.w: One first reading (184) was 180 or higher, so he re-measured after 5 minutes. The repeat (182) was still 180 or higher. He has none of the listed symptoms, so the "otherwise" branch applies: call the office right away.

n.1: He has already waited and re-measured once, as directed; the instructions do not call for a further wait.
n.2: This applies when both readings are between 140 and 179; his were 184 and 176, and the repeat was 182.
n.3: Calling 911 applies only with chest pain, shortness of breath or trouble speaking, and he has none of these.

R.q:
While studying for an anatomy quiz, Rosa comes across the word epistaxis in her textbook. The chapter uses the word several times but never shows how to say it. Tomorrow she will present a case study to her study group, and she wants to pronounce the word correctly and confirm whether it is a noun or a verb before she uses it.

Which source would best help Rosa?
o: The index of her textbook
An almanac of health statistics
A thesaurus of medical terms
A medical dictionary
R.w: A dictionary gives a word's pronunciation, part of speech, and definition, which is exactly what Rosa needs.

n.0: An index lists the pages where a term appears; it does not show pronunciation or part of speech.
n.1: An almanac compiles facts and figures, not word pronunciations.
n.2: A thesaurus lists words with similar meanings; it is not the place to find pronunciation.

R.q:
Follow the directions.

Six chairs stand in a row, numbered 1 to 6 from left to right. Ana sits in chair 1, Ben in chair 2, Cruz in chair 3, Dev in chair 4, Eli in chair 5 and Fay in chair 6. Carry out the steps below in order.
1. Ana and Fay trade seats.
2. The person in chair 3 trades seats with the person in chair 5.
3. The person sitting immediately to the right of Ben trades seats with Ana.
4. Dev trades seats with whoever is in chair 1.

Who sits in chairs 1 through 6 after step 4?
o: Dev, Ben, Ana, Fay, Eli, Cruz
Fay, Ben, Dev, Ana, Cruz, Eli
Dev, Ben, Ana, Fay, Cruz, Eli
Dev, Ben, Eli, Ana, Cruz, Fay
R.w: Step 1: Fay, Ben, Cruz, Dev, Eli, Ana. Step 2 swaps chairs 3 and 5: Fay, Ben, Eli, Dev, Cruz, Ana. Step 3: Eli is right of Ben and trades with Ana: Fay, Ben, Ana, Dev, Cruz, Eli. Step 4: Dev trades with Fay in chair 1: Dev, Ben, Ana, Fay, Cruz, Eli.

n.0: Skips step 2, so Cruz and Eli never trade seats.
n.1: Has Dev trade with Ana, who started in chair 1, instead of whoever is in chair 1 after step 3.
n.3: Uses the person to the left of Ben (Fay) in step 3 instead of the person to the right.

R.q:
Read the passage.

For most of the twentieth century, the Harlan textile mill employed nearly half the working adults in Pine Ridge. When the mill closed in 1998, hundreds of families moved away to find work, and the town's population dropped by a third within five years.

With fewer children enrolled, the district merged Pine Ridge's two elementary schools into one. The empty building sat unused until 2015, when a group of residents raised money to turn it into a community health center.

Today the center employs forty people, and its staff includes several former students of the old school.

Which is the best summary of the passage?
o: Pine Ridge lost a third of its people after the district merged its two elementary schools, which led the mill to close.
Residents of Pine Ridge raised money in 2015 to build a new community health center that now employs forty people.
After the mill closed and families left, Pine Ridge merged its schools, and residents turned the empty one into a clinic.
The Harlan textile mill employed nearly half of Pine Ridge's working adults for most of the twentieth century.
R.w: The passage is a chain of causes and effects: the mill closed, families left, enrollment fell, the schools merged, and residents later turned the empty school into a health center. This option keeps that chain in the correct order.

n.0: Reverses cause and effect: the mill closing caused the population loss, which led to the school merger, not the other way around.
n.1: Distortion: residents converted the old school building rather than building a new center, and the option skips the cause.
n.3: Too narrow: this is background from the first sentence only.

R.q:
Survey of 400 volunteers at Grandview Hospital: "How did you first hear about our volunteer program?"
Friend or family member | 45%
Hospital website | 25%
Social media | 20%
Newspaper ad | 10%

At a planning meeting, the volunteer coordinator said she wants to spend most of next year's outreach budget on newspaper ads. "The newspaper brought in 40 volunteers," she said, "which is more than we expected."

Which statement best combines the survey results with the coordinator's statement?
o: Her figure of 40 conflicts with the survey, which shows only 10.
Her 40 volunteers are accurate but are the smallest group in the survey.
The newspaper brought in more volunteers than social media did.
Most volunteers first heard about the program through online sources.
R.w: Ten percent of 400 is 40, so her figure matches the survey. But the newspaper is the smallest source; friends and family (180), the website (100), and social media (80) each brought in more volunteers.

n.0: This treats 10 percent as a count; 10 percent of 400 volunteers is 40, matching her figure.
n.2: Social media accounts for 20 percent, or 80 volunteers, twice the newspaper's 40.
n.3: The website and social media together make up 45 percent, which is less than half.

R.q:
Read the passage.

Ana's shift at the animal shelter began at six, but she arrived at five-thirty every Saturday so that she could walk Biscuit before the other volunteers came in. Biscuit, a gray pit bull mix, had lived at the shelter for fourteen months, longer than any other dog. Visitors usually walked past his kennel because he barked at strangers, and twice he had been returned by families who adopted him. With Ana, though, he sat for treats and walked calmly on his leash. One Saturday, Ana brought her roommate along and asked her to hold the leash. Biscuit sniffed the roommate's shoes, then sat. Ana smiled and took a photo for the shelter's website.

Which of the following can be inferred from the passage? Select all that apply.
o: Biscuit was returned twice because he bit a member of a family.
Ana has formed a close bond with Biscuit.
Biscuit is the oldest of the dogs currently living at the shelter.
Ana hopes to improve Biscuit's chances of being adopted.
Biscuit behaves better with familiar people than with strangers.
Ana's roommate is nervous around large dogs she has not met before.
R.w: Ana comes early every week to walk Biscuit, so they are close. He barks at strangers but is calm with Ana, so he is better with people he knows. Testing him with a new person and posting a calm photo on the shelter's website suggest she wants to help him find a home.

n.0: The passage says he was returned twice but never gives a reason; a bite is an assumption.
n.2: Distortion: Biscuit has been at the shelter the longest, which says nothing about his age.
n.5: Nothing describes the roommate's feelings; she simply holds the leash.

R.q:
Read the passage.

Hospitals are noisier than most people expect. Alarms from monitors and pumps, overhead pages, rolling carts and conversations at nursing stations can push nighttime sound levels well above what sleep researchers recommend for bedrooms.

The noise matters because sleep is part of recovery. Patients who sleep poorly in the hospital often report more pain and more confusion, and they may be slower to regain strength. Staff are affected as well: frequent alarms that turn out to be harmless can lead nurses to respond more slowly to the ones that count.

Some hospitals have tried quiet hours, softer flooring and alarms that alert only the assigned nurse's phone. A few units report better patient sleep scores, although the changes can be costly to install.

Which is the best summary of the passage?
o: Changes such as softer flooring and phone-based alarms are costly for hospitals to install on their units.
Frequent harmless alarms can lead nurses to respond more slowly to the alarms that signal real problems.
Hospitals are noisier than people expect because of monitors, pages, carts and conversations at stations.
Hospital noise disrupts patient sleep and staff response, and some hospitals are testing ways to reduce it.
R.w: Paragraph 1 describes the noise, paragraph 2 explains why it matters for patients and staff, and paragraph 3 describes efforts to reduce it. This option combines all three with the same emphasis as the passage.

n.0: Reversed emphasis: the cost of the changes is a brief qualification at the very end, not the passage's central point.
n.1: Too narrow: alarm fatigue is one detail in the second paragraph.
n.2: Summarizes only the first paragraph and leaves out why the noise matters and what hospitals are doing.

R.q:
Email from Dana Price: The CPR instructor training starts at 9:00 a.m. on Thursday at the County Health Building on Fifth Street. Please arrive 15 minutes early to sign in and pick up your materials. The building is a 10-minute walk from the Fifth Street bus stop.

Route 12 weekday schedule, arrival times at Fifth Street
7:52 a.m. | 8:22 a.m. | 8:37 a.m. | 8:52 a.m. | 9:07 a.m.

Omar is taking Route 12 to the training. Based on the email and the schedule, which is the latest bus he can take and still arrive in time to sign in?
o: The 8:52 a.m. bus
The 8:37 a.m. bus
The 7:52 a.m. bus
The 8:22 a.m. bus
R.w: Step 1: arriving 15 minutes before 9:00 means being at the building by 8:45. Step 2: with a 10-minute walk, the bus must reach Fifth Street by 8:35. The latest bus that does is the 8:22.

n.0: The 8:52 bus plus the walk arrives at 9:02, which misses sign-in and is late for the start.
n.1: The 8:37 bus plus a 10-minute walk reaches the building at 8:47, after the 8:45 sign-in time.
n.2: The 7:52 bus works, but the question asks for the latest bus that still gets him there in time.

R.q:
For a paper on nursing during the American Civil War, Andre is using two sources.
Source A: the diary kept by a volunteer nurse at a Union hospital in Washington, D.C., from 1862 to 1864
Source B: a 2015 book by a historian who compares the diaries of 30 Civil War nurses and explains what they reveal about hospital conditions
His bibliography must label each source correctly.

Which statement correctly classifies both sources?
o: Source A is secondary, and Source B is primary.
Both are primary, since Source B quotes diaries.
Source A is primary, and Source B is secondary.
Source A is primary, and Source B is tertiary.
R.w: Step 1: the diary is a firsthand account written at the time, so Source A is primary. Step 2: the historian's book analyzes and interprets those diaries, so Source B is secondary.

n.0: This reverses the categories: the diary is the firsthand record, and the book interprets it.
n.1: Quoting primary sources does not make a book primary; its author interprets others' accounts.
n.3: Source B offers original analysis; tertiary sources such as encyclopedias only compile summaries.

R.q:
Coach Rivera paced the sideline, certain that his team had one more good play left in them. On the bench, Tyler rubbed his sore ankle and hoped the coach would not notice, because he wanted desperately to finish the game. In the stands, Tyler's mother gripped her program and wondered whether she should have let him play at all. And the referee, who had made a questionable call in the first half, quietly promised himself that he would get the next one right.

Which point of view does the author use?
o: third person objective
first person, told by an observer
third person limited
third person omniscient
R.w: The narrator stands outside the story and reveals the private thoughts of four different people: the coach, Tyler, his mother and the referee. Knowing the minds of many characters is third person omniscient.

n.0: An objective narrator reports only what can be seen and heard, but this narrator tells us what each person hopes, wonders and promises privately.
n.1: No narrator refers to himself or herself as "I," not even an onlooker; every character is described from outside.
n.2: A limited narrator reveals one character's thoughts; this one moves freely among several.

R.q:
Read the passage.

At exactly 10:00 a.m., the fire alarm sounded on the fourth floor of Lincoln Hospital. At that same moment, the automatic fire doors swung shut, and every elevator returned to the ground floor and stopped. Nurses on the unit then closed the doors to patient rooms, beginning with the rooms closest to the stairwell. Two minutes later, the charge nurse called the operator to report that the unit was secure. The all-clear sounded at 10:12, after which the elevators were returned to service and the fire doors were reopened.

According to the passage, which event happened immediately after the elevators returned to the ground floor?
o: Nurses closed the doors to patient rooms.
The charge nurse called the hospital operator.
The automatic fire doors on the unit swung shut.
The all-clear sounded at 10:12.
R.w: The alarm, the fire doors and the elevators all acted "at that same moment." The next event, signaled by "then," is the nurses closing patient room doors.

n.1: The call to the operator came two minutes after the nurses closed the room doors.
n.2: The fire doors closed at the same moment as the elevators returned, not after.
n.3: The all-clear came at 10:12, several events later.

R.q:
Read the passage.

In 1928, Alexander Fleming returned from a vacation to find mold growing on one of his plates of bacteria, with a clear ring around it where the bacteria had died. He named the substance the mold produced penicillin, but he could not purify it in useful amounts. About a decade later, Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford took up the problem, and in 1940 they showed that penicillin protected infected mice. The first human patients were treated in 1941. Mass production in the United States during World War II made the drug widely available by 1944, and the three scientists shared the Nobel Prize in 1945.

Which statement about the order of events is accurate?
o: The first human patients were treated before the mouse experiments.
Florey and Chain purified penicillin before Fleming gave it a name.
Mice were protected by penicillin a year before people were treated.
The Nobel Prize was awarded before mass production of the drug began.
R.w: The mouse experiments were in 1940 and the first human patients were treated in 1941, one year later.

n.0: Reverses the order: mice in 1940, people in 1941.
n.1: Reverses the order: Fleming named penicillin in 1928, about a decade before Florey and Chain began their work.
n.3: Reverses the order: wartime mass production made the drug widely available by 1944, and the prize came in 1945.

R.q:
Read the glossary from a patient guide.

Glossary
Benign: not cancerous; does not spread to other parts of the body.
Biopsy: removal of a small sample of tissue to be examined under a microscope.
Malignant: cancerous; able to invade nearby tissue and spread.
Metastasis: the spread of cancer from the place where it started to another part of the body.
Oncologist: a doctor who specializes in treating cancer.
Remission: a decrease in or disappearance of the signs of cancer.

A patient's report reads, "The biopsy showed a benign growth." Based on the glossary, what does this sentence mean?
o: Signs of cancer in the growth have decreased since the last exam.
A doctor who treats cancer found a growth that needs a closer look.
A tissue sample showed cancer that has spread to another part of the body.
A tissue sample showed a growth that is not cancerous.
R.w: A biopsy is a tissue sample examined under a microscope, and benign means not cancerous. Together: the sample showed a growth that is not cancer.

n.0: This describes remission, a different glossary term.
n.1: This confuses biopsy with oncologist; a biopsy is a tissue sample, not a doctor.
n.2: This combines malignant and metastasis, the terms that describe cancer that spreads.

R.q:
A health blogger claims that a 20-minute nap in mid-afternoon makes office workers more alert for the rest of the day. As evidence, she cites a poll of 300 of her readers: 82 percent of those who nap regularly said they feel sharper after a nap. She recommends that employers set aside quiet rooms where workers can sleep during their afternoon breaks.

Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the blogger's claim?
o: Most of the blogger's readers who nap regularly say they enjoy taking naps.
Several famous inventors and leaders were known to take short daytime naps.
Workers who nap for an hour or more often report feeling groggy after waking.
Workers chosen at random to nap scored higher on alertness tests than non-nappers.
R.w: The blogger's evidence is a self-selected poll of how readers feel. A study that randomly assigns workers to nap and measures alertness with tests provides stronger, controlled evidence for the same claim.

n.0: Enjoying naps is not the same as being more alert, so this adds nothing to the claim.
n.1: Famous examples are anecdotes, not evidence that naps raise alertness in office workers.
n.2: This concerns long naps, not the 20-minute naps in the claim, and it does not show any benefit.

R.q:
Read the passage.

The Westbrook Public Health Department offered free flu shots at three locations last October. The downtown clinic, open weekdays from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m., gave 410 shots. A kiosk at the mall, open weekday evenings and all day on weekends, gave 1,280. A mobile van that parked outside large workplaces at lunchtime gave 960. This year the department has the same budget and staff, and it plans to close one of the three locations.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
o: Many residents found it easier to get a shot outside standard weekday business hours.
Residents who live downtown were less worried about the flu than residents elsewhere.
Most residents would rather get a flu shot at work than at a clinic or a mall.
The department will close the mall kiosk because it costs the most to operate.
R.w: The location open evenings and weekends gave the most shots (1,280), more than three times the weekday-hours clinic (410). That pattern best supports the conclusion that many people found off-hours more convenient.

n.1: Unsupported: the downtown clinic's location and hours explain the lower number as well as any attitude; the passage says nothing about worry.
n.2: Overreaches: the workplace van gave fewer shots (960) than the mall kiosk, so "most residents" prefer work is not supported.
n.3: Unsupported: the passage gives no costs and does not say which location will close.

R.q:
Read the procedure.

In a Fire Emergency, Unit 5
If you see fire or smoke, first remove any patient in immediate danger from the room. Then activate the nearest alarm pull station, unless the alarm is already sounding. Next, close the doors to all patient rooms and stairwells. After closing the doors, report to the nurses' station and give the charge nurse the room number of any patient you moved. Do not use the elevators. If the charge nurse orders an evacuation, move patients horizontally through the fire doors to the next unit before considering the stairs.

Kayla, a nursing assistant, sees smoke coming from room 512. The alarm is silent, and one patient is in the room. Later, the charge nurse orders an evacuation.

Place Kayla's actions in the order the procedure requires, starting with the first.
o: Move patients through the fire doors to the next unit
Close the doors to patient rooms and stairwells
Activate the nearest alarm pull station
Move the patient out of room 512
Give the charge nurse the room number at the nurses' station
R.w: The procedure's order is: remove the patient in danger first; then pull the alarm (required here because the alarm is silent); then close doors; then report the moved patient's room number; and finally, because the charge nurse orders an evacuation, move patients horizontally through the fire doors.

R.q:
For a child development class, Tyler wrote a report arguing that parents should limit preschoolers' screen time to two hours a day. His only source is a 1999 pamphlet from a parenting group, printed before most families owned smartphones or tablets. The pamphlet discusses television viewing and recommends the two-hour limit. Tyler did not check whether the group or any health agency has updated its advice since then.

What is the main weakness of the evidence Tyler uses?
o: It is unrelated to the subject of screen time for preschool children.
It comes from a source with a financial interest in the advice it gives.
It is too dated for a topic on which guidance may have since changed.
It is a personal story about one child rather than general guidance.
R.w: The pamphlet is from 1999, before smartphones and tablets were common, and Tyler never checked for updated advice. For a fast-changing topic, an old source lacks currency.

n.0: The pamphlet addresses children's screen viewing, so it is related to the topic.
n.1: The passage gives no sign that the parenting group profits from its advice.
n.3: The pamphlet offers a general recommendation, not one child's story.

R.q:
The blue light from phones and tablets signals the brain to stay awake, and a 2023 survey found that children who used screens in the hour before bed slept 40 minutes less on school nights than children who did not. Tired children struggle to pay attention in class and are more likely to be irritable. Parents, it is time to act. Set a family rule that all screens go into a basket in the kitchen one hour before bedtime, and follow the rule yourselves.

Which of the following best states the author's purpose?
o: to discuss the topic of children's sleep and electronic devices
to report the results of a 2023 survey about children's screen use
to describe a typical bedtime routine in an American family
to convince parents to limit children's screen use before bed
R.w: The passage builds to direct commands ("Parents, it is time to act. Set a family rule..."), so its purpose is to convince parents to take a specific action.

n.0: This names the topic, not the purpose. It leaves out the author's clear push for a particular action.
n.1: The survey is one piece of supporting evidence; the passage does not report its methods or full results.
n.2: The basket in the kitchen is a recommendation, not a description of what families already do.

R.q:
Council member Reyes has proposed closing two blocks of Main Street to cars on Saturday mornings from May through September so that a farmers market can set up. Her opponent responded: "Reyes wants to ban cars from downtown. If she had her way, delivery trucks could not reach our stores, and shoppers who drive would have nowhere to go. I cannot support a plan that shuts down our business district."

Which statement best describes the flaw in the opponent's response?
o: It claims the plan is good or bad based on how many people favor it.
It attacks an exaggerated version of the plan instead of the real one.
It attacks Reyes's character instead of discussing her proposal.
It presents two choices as the only ones when others exist.
R.w: Reyes proposed closing two blocks on summer Saturday mornings, but the opponent describes a ban on cars downtown and argues against that. Misrepresenting a position to make it easier to attack is a straw man.

n.0: The response never mentions public opinion or popularity.
n.2: The opponent criticizes a (distorted) plan, not Reyes's character, so this is not ad hominem.
n.3: The response does not reduce the issue to two options; it rejects a misdescribed plan.

R.q:
For a nursing history assignment, Jordan chose a 1998 biography of Ada Whitfield, a nurse who opened her county's first public health clinic in 1912. The author, a historian, spent ten years studying Whitfield's clinic records, newspaper notices, and letters written by people who knew her, and the book quotes many of these documents. Jordan labeled the biography a primary source in his bibliography.

Why is Jordan's label incorrect?
o: The biography is tertiary because it covers Whitfield's entire life and career.
The biography was published long after Whitfield's death, so it cannot be primary.
The author did not live these events and interprets them from records.
The book quotes letters and notices instead of reporting the author's own views.
R.w: A biography is a secondary source because its author did not experience the events but interprets primary sources such as clinic records, newspaper notices, and letters.

n.0: Tertiary sources compile brief summaries (encyclopedias, almanacs); a researched biography is secondary.
n.1: Date alone does not decide the category; a memoir written decades later is still primary. What matters is that the author interprets others' records.
n.3: Quoting primary documents does not make a book primary, and the author does offer interpretation.

R.q:
I was twenty-three when I lost my first patient. Mr. Alvarez had told me about his grandchildren every morning for two weeks, and I had promised to see the photos his daughter was bringing on Friday. He died on Thursday night. I followed every step I had been taught: I called the physician, notified the family and prepared the body with care. Then I sat in the supply room and cried. Twenty years later, I still think of him whenever a patient starts to tell me about the people they love.

What is the author's primary purpose in this passage?
o: to persuade hospitals to offer grief counseling to nurses
to express the author's feelings about a past experience
to inform new nurses about the steps to follow after a death
to entertain readers with a suspenseful hospital story
R.w: The first-person reflection, the detail about the photos and the admission that the author cried and still remembers the patient all show a writer sharing personal feelings. Expressing emotion about an experience is the purpose.

n.0: The passage never mentions counseling or asks hospitals to do anything.
n.2: The steps after a death are mentioned in a single sentence as part of the memory; they are not explained in a way meant to teach.
n.3: The story is moving rather than suspenseful, and it is told to share feelings rather than to amuse or thrill.

R.q:
Follow the directions.

Start with the number 386. Carry out the steps below in order, applying each step to the result of the step before it.
1. Add the digits together, and write the sum directly after the original number (for example, 213 would become 2136).
2. Remove every digit that is greater than 6.
3. Reverse the order of the digits.
4. Subtract 63.
5. Divide by 4.

What is the final result?

n.2: Skips step 1, so 386 becomes 36, then 63, then 0.
n.3: Writes the sum before the number (17386), giving 136, then 631, 568 and 142.

R.q:
Charge nurse Angela Morris is writing an annual review for Kayla Brooks, a nurse on her unit. When a patient's pain medication is late or a test result is missing, Kayla calls the pharmacy or the lab again and again until the problem is solved. Angela wants the review to praise this habit. She drafts the sentence, "Kayla is ______ when she advocates for her patients."

Which word best completes the sentence in a way that matches Angela's purpose?
o: obstinate
nagging
pushy
tenacious
R.w: All four words describe someone who keeps pressing, so their denotations overlap. Only "tenacious" carries a positive connotation (admirably determined), which fits a sentence meant to praise.

n.0: "Obstinate" suggests unreasonable stubbornness, a negative connotation that would criticize rather than praise.
n.1: "Nagging" suggests annoying, repeated complaining, which is negative.
n.2: "Pushy" describes the same behavior with a negative connotation of being rude or overbearing.

R.q:
Read the label.

Nutrition Facts
Servings per container: 3
Serving size: 1 cup (240 mL)
Amount per serving
Calories: 150
Total Fat: 4 g (5% Daily Value)
Sodium: 480 mg (21% Daily Value)
Total Carbohydrate: 22 g (8% Daily Value)
   Dietary Fiber: 5 g (18% Daily Value)
   Total Sugars: 6 g
Protein: 7 g
Ingredients: water, black beans, tomatoes, onions, corn, salt, chili powder, garlic.

Keisha heats the soup and eats two servings. Based on the label, how much sodium does she consume?
o: 42 mg
480 mg
960 mg
R.w: Label amounts are per serving. Keisha eats 2 servings, so 2 x 480 mg = 960 mg of sodium.

n.0: Doubles the 21% Daily Value and treats the 42 as milligrams.
n.1: 480 mg is the amount in one serving, but Keisha eats two.
n.3: 1,440 mg is the sodium in the whole container (3 servings), not in the 2 servings she eats.

R.q:
Read the passage.

Many people believe that food dropped on the floor is safe to eat if it is picked up within five seconds. Researchers who tested this idea dropped several foods, including watermelon, bread and gummy candy, onto surfaces coated with harmless bacteria. Bacteria reached some foods in less than one second. Time on the floor did matter, since longer contact transferred more bacteria, but the type of food mattered more. Wet watermelon picked up the most bacteria, while gummy candy picked up the least. The surface mattered too: carpet passed fewer bacteria to food than tile or stainless steel did. Speed, it turns out, is a poor guide to whether dropped food is clean.

Which title best fits the passage?
o: Testing the Five-Second Rule
How Bacteria Spread Through the Home
The Five-Second Rule Holds Up in the Lab
Watermelon: The Riskiest Food to Drop
R.w: A good title names the topic and fits the whole passage. The passage describes an experiment that tested the five-second belief and concludes that speed is a poor guide, so "Testing the Five-Second Rule" covers the entire text.

n.1: Too broad: the passage covers transfer from a floor surface to dropped food, not bacteria throughout a home.
n.2: Opposite of the passage: bacteria transferred in under one second, so the rule did not hold up.
n.3: Too narrow: watermelon is one result within the experiment, not the subject of the whole passage.

R.q:
Read the passage.

In January, Lakeside Clinic launched a phone app that sends patients appointment reminders. Missed appointments fell from 18 percent in December to 11 percent in March. In February, the clinic also began calling every patient the day before a visit, and it moved its Monday appointments, historically the most often missed, to later in the morning. The clinic manager praised the app in the staff newsletter.

A reader concludes that the app alone caused missed appointments to fall. Which detail from the passage shows that this conclusion goes beyond the evidence?
o: The clinic also began calling every patient the day before.
Missed appointments fell from 18 percent to 11 percent by March.
The clinic launched its reminder app in January of that year.
The app sends patients reminders before their appointments.
R.w: The phone calls began during the same period the drop occurred, so they are another possible cause. A conclusion that the app alone was responsible ignores this competing explanation.

n.1: The size of the drop shows that something worked, not which change caused it.
n.2: The launch date fits the app being a cause; it does not show the conclusion overreaches.
n.3: Describing what the app does is consistent with the conclusion; it does not challenge it.

R.q:
Our school district's plan to give every high school student a free tablet has real promise. Students without computers at home would finally be able to complete online assignments, and teachers could share lessons more easily. Still, I have questions. The district has not explained who will repair broken devices, and it has budgeted no money for training teachers to use them well. If those gaps are filled before the fall, I will be among the plan's strongest supporters.

Which of the following best describes the author's attitude toward the tablet plan?
o: opposed, with a few exceptions
supportive, with reservations
enthusiastic, with no concerns
neutral, with no stated view
R.w: The author praises the plan's "real promise" but raises questions about repairs and training, and promises full support only if those gaps are filled. Support with conditions is a qualified, or cautiously supportive, attitude.

n.0: The author's main stance is favorable; the concerns are conditions for full support, not reasons to oppose the plan.
n.2: The author raises two specific concerns, so the support is not unqualified.
n.3: The author clearly expresses a view ("real promise," "I have questions"), so the passage is not neutral.

R.q:
Passage 1
From the school nurse: Students who eat breakfast tend to pay closer attention during morning classes. But not every breakfast helps equally. A meal with protein and whole grains, such as eggs and toast, keeps energy steady until lunch, while a frosted pastry often leads to a slump by mid-morning.

Passage 2
From a nutrition column: Studies on breakfast and body weight have produced mixed results, and skipping breakfast does not appear to cause weight gain by itself. What people eat over the whole day matters more. A sugary muffin at 7 a.m. is no better a choice than waiting until a balanced lunch.

Which idea is expressed in both passages?
o: The kind of food eaten matters, not simply whether a meal is eaten.
Eating breakfast improves students' attention during morning classes.
Skipping breakfast has little effect on a person's body weight.
Breakfast is the most important meal of the day for good health.
R.w: Passage 1 contrasts eggs and toast with a frosted pastry; Passage 2 says a sugary muffin is no better than waiting for a balanced lunch. Both stress food quality over the fact of eating.

n.1: This is the central claim of Passage 1 only; Passage 2 does not discuss attention.
n.2: This comes from Passage 2 only; Passage 1 does not discuss weight.
n.3: Neither passage says this; Passage 2 suggests breakfast is not essential for weight.

M.q: A double bar graph shows hospital admissions by unit in 2024 and 2025: Cardiac 320 and 368; Orthopedics 250 and 275; Pediatrics 180 and 216; Oncology 400 and 436. Which unit had the greatest percent increase in admissions from 2024 to 2025?
o: Cardiac
Oncology
Orthopedics
Pediatrics
M.w: Percent increase = change / 2024 value. Cardiac 48 / 320 = 15%. Orthopedics 25 / 250 = 10%. Pediatrics 36 / 180 = 20%. Oncology 36 / 400 = 9%. Pediatrics is greatest.

n.0: Cardiac had the largest increase in number (48), but 48 / 320 is only 15%.
n.1: Oncology has the tallest bars, but its 36 extra admissions are only 9% of 400.
n.2: Orthopedics rose 25 / 250 = 10%.

M.q: A multidose vial contains 20 mL of medication, and 4.5 mL has already been drawn from it. Each dose is 1.5 mL. How many more full doses can be drawn from the vial?
M.w: Medication left: 20 - 4.5 = 15.5 mL. Doses: 15.5 ÷ 1.5 = 10.33. Only complete doses count, so round down: 10 full doses (10 × 1.5 = 15 mL; 0.5 mL is left over).

n.1: 14 ignores the 4.5 mL already drawn and also rounds 13.33 up instead of down.
n.2: 11 rounds 10.33 up; 11 doses would need 16.5 mL, but only 15.5 mL is left.
n.3: 13 ignores the 4.5 mL already drawn (20 ÷ 1.5 = 13.33, rounded down).

M.q: Ava drove 168 miles to a nursing school open house in 3 hours 30 minutes. What was her average speed for the drive?
o: 42 miles per hour
50.9 miles per hour
56 miles per hour
48 miles per hour
M.w: 3 hours 30 minutes = 3.5 hours. Speed = distance ÷ time = 168 ÷ 3.5 = 48 miles per hour.

n.0: This rounds the time up to 4 hours before dividing.
n.1: This reads 3 hours 30 minutes as 3.30 hours. Thirty minutes is 0.5 hour, so the time is 3.5 hours.
n.2: This divides by 3 hours and ignores the extra 30 minutes.

M.q: A histogram of household incomes in a town has a tall peak on the left and a long tail stretching to the right. Which statement about the incomes is most likely true?
o: The mean and median are about equal
The distribution is skewed to the left
The mean is greater than the median
The median is greater than the mean
M.w: A long tail to the right is a right (positive) skew. The few very high incomes pull the mean toward the tail, so the mean is greater than the median.

n.0: Mean and median are about equal in a symmetric distribution, not a skewed one.
n.1: Skew is named for the tail, not the peak; the tail here is on the right.
n.3: That relationship fits a left-skewed distribution, where the tail is on the low side.

M.q: The daily patient census on a medical unit for one week was 28, 31, 24, 35, 29, 22, and 33. What is the range of the daily census for the week?
M.w: Range = maximum - minimum = 35 - 22 = 13.

n.0: 33 - 28 = 5 subtracts the first value from the last as listed, not the minimum from the maximum.
n.2: 35 - 24 = 11 uses 24 as the minimum, but 22 is smaller.
n.3: 31 - 22 = 9 uses 31 as the maximum, but 35 is larger.

M.q: Tyrese buys nursing shoes and a watch for a combined $248 before tax. The sales tax rate is 7.25%. What is his total cost including tax? Enter the amount in dollars, to the nearest cent.

tr.17.98: Found the tax alone instead of the total cost.

M.q: A morning section of 12 students had a mean quiz score of 75, and an afternoon section of 28 students had a mean quiz score of 85. What is the mean quiz score of all 40 students?

n.0: (12 x 85 + 28 x 75) / 40 = 78 swaps the section sizes.
n.1: The larger section pulls the mean toward 85, but the 12 lower scores still count.
n.3: (75 + 85) / 2 = 80 averages the two means, ignoring that the sections have different sizes.

M.q: A county's sales tax rate is stored in a spreadsheet as the decimal 0.0375. What is this tax rate written as a percent? Enter the number only, without the percent sign.

tr.0.375: Moved the decimal point only 1 place right.
tr.37.5: Moved the decimal point 3 places right.

M.w: To change a decimal to a percent, multiply by 100 (move the decimal point 2 places right): 0.0375 × 100 = 3.75, so the rate is 3.75%.

M.q: A hospital department logged 2,749.5 overtime hours last year. What is 2,749.5 rounded to the nearest hundred?
M.w: The hundreds digit is 7. Look only at the digit to its right (tens), which is 4, so keep 7: 2,700.

n.0: 2,800 rounds in two steps (2,749.5 → 2,750 → 2,800). Round once, using the tens digit.
n.2: 2,750 rounds to the nearest ten, not the nearest hundred.
n.3: 3,000 rounds to the nearest thousand.

M.q: Jordan earns $2,850 per month. He puts 12% of his earnings into a retirement account and 8% into a savings account. How much of his monthly earnings is left after both?
M.w: Both are percents of the same $2,850, so they add: 12% + 8% = 20% set aside, leaving 80%. 0.80 × 2,850 = $2,280.

n.0: This subtracts the 12% retirement contribution but not the 8% savings.
n.2: This subtracts the 8% savings but not the 12% retirement contribution.
n.3: This is the 20% set aside, not the amount left.

M.q: A child's dose of a liquid medicine, M, in milliliters, is calculated from the child's weight, W, in kilograms, using the formula M = 0.4W. Which statement is correct?
o: M is independent, because the dose is what the nurse controls
M is independent, and W rises by 2 kg when M rises by 5 mL
W is independent, and M rises by 12.5 mL when W rises by 5 kg
W is independent, and M rises by 2 mL when W rises by 5 kg
M.w: The dose is calculated from the weight, so W is independent and M is dependent. An increase of 5 kg changes M by 0.4 x 5 = 2 mL.

n.0: The dose is the output of the formula; the weight is the input.
n.1: This swaps the variables; the dose is calculated from the weight.
n.2: 5 / 0.4 = 12.5 divides by the rate instead of multiplying: 0.4 x 5 = 2 mL.

M.q: A researcher has recorded each of 40 adults' average daily calorie intake and their change in weight over one month. Which display best shows whether the two variables are related?
o: Line graph
Scatterplot
Double bar graph
Circle graph
M.w: A scatterplot plots one point per adult using two numeric variables, which shows whether they tend to rise or fall together.

n.0: A line graph tracks change over time, but these data pair two measurements for each person.
n.2: A double bar graph compares two series across categories, and 40 individual adults are not categories to compare.
n.3: A circle graph shows parts of a whole, not a relationship between two variables.

M.q: Which inequality is the solution of -3 < 2x + 5 ≤ 11?
M.w: Subtract 5 from all three parts: -8 < 2x ≤ 6. Divide all three parts by 2: -4 < x ≤ 3.

n.1: This swaps the symbols. The left boundary is strict (<), and the right boundary includes 3 (≤).
n.2: This subtracts 5 from all three parts but does not divide by 2.
n.3: This adds 5 to all three parts instead of subtracting, giving 2 < 2x ≤ 16.

M.q: A hospital pharmacy receives 1,200 vials of a vaccine. It sends 3/8 of the vials to the intensive care unit, and then sends 2/5 of the remaining vials to the emergency department. How many vials are left in the pharmacy?
M.w: ICU: 3/8 × 1,200 = 450, leaving 750. Emergency department: 2/5 × 750 = 300. Left: 750 - 300 = 450 vials.

n.0: 300 is the number sent to the emergency department, not the number left.
n.2: 750 is the number left after the first step, before the emergency department's share.
n.3: 270 takes 2/5 of the original 1,200 (480) instead of 2/5 of the remaining 750.

M.q: Sam's gym membership costs $35 per month, and a personal trainer charges $45 per session. Sam budgets no more than $400 per month for the gym and training combined. What is the greatest number of training sessions he can book in a month? Enter a whole number.

tr.9: Rounded up; 9 sessions plus the membership cost $440, which is over budget.

M.w: Write 35 + 45s ≤ 400. Subtract 35: 45s ≤ 365. Divide by 45: s ≤ 8.11. The greatest whole number is 8 (35 + 360 = $395).

M.q: A table summarizes a screening test given to 500 people. Tested positive and have the condition: 45. Tested positive and do not have the condition: 15. Tested negative and have the condition: 5. Tested negative and do not have the condition: 435. Of the people who tested positive, what percent actually have the condition? Enter the number only.

tr.12: the percent of all 500 people who tested positive
tr.90: 45 out of the 50 people who have the condition

M.w: 'Of the people who tested positive' sets the denominator: 45 + 15 = 60. Of these, 45 have the condition. 45 / 60 = 0.75 = 75%.

M.q: A student in a prerequisite math course evaluates the expression 5² + 3 × 2³ - √64 by hand. What is the value of the expression? Enter the number only.
M.w: Exponents and roots first: 5² = 25, 2³ = 8 and √64 = 8. Multiply: 3 × 8 = 24. Then add and subtract left to right: 25 + 24 - 8 = 41.

M.q: Kayla completed 0.875 of her required clinical observation hours by the end of October. Which fraction, written in lowest terms, is equivalent to 0.875?
M.w: 0.875 has three decimal places: 875/1,000. The GCF of 875 and 1,000 is 125, so 875/1,000 = 7/8.

n.0: 7/80 = 0.0875, ten times smaller than 0.875.
n.1: 87/100 = 0.87; it drops the thousandths digit instead of converting the full decimal.
n.3: 35/40 equals 0.875, but it is not in lowest terms; 35 and 40 still share a factor of 5.

M.q: A patient on a fluid restriction may drink no more than 1,800 milliliters per day. By early afternoon, the patient has had 3 cups of coffee and 10 fluid ounces of water. Use 1 cup = 240 milliliters and 1 fluid ounce = 30 milliliters. How many more milliliters may the patient drink today?
o: 980 mL
780 mL
M.w: Coffee: 3 × 240 = 720 mL. Water: 10 × 30 = 300 mL. Total so far = 1,020 mL. Remaining = 1,800 - 1,020 = 780 mL.

n.0: 1,020 mL is the amount already taken; subtract it from 1,800 mL.
n.1: This counts 10 fl oz as 100 mL; 10 × 30 = 300 mL.
n.2: This subtracts the coffee (720 mL) but leaves out the 10 fl oz of water.

M.q: A roll of medical tape is 5 yards long. A nurse cuts strips that are each 8 inches long to secure dressings. How many complete 8-inch strips can be cut from the roll?
M.w: 5 yd × 36 in per yd = 180 in. 180 ÷ 8 = 22.5, so 22 complete strips can be cut.

n.0: This uses 12 inches per yard (5 yd = 60 in); 1 yd = 36 in.
n.1: 180 ÷ 8 = 22.5, and half a strip is not a complete strip, so round down.
n.3: This uses 10 inches per foot (15 ft = 150 in); 1 ft = 12 in.

M.q: The wait times, in minutes, for seven patients at an urgent care center were 12, 14, 14, 16, 17, 18, and 65. Which measure best describes a typical wait time for these patients, and why?
o: The mean, because it uses every value in the data set
The median, because the 65-minute wait pulls the mean up
The range, because it shows the spread from 12 to 65
The mode, because 14 is the most common wait time
M.w: The mean is 156 / 7 = 22.3 minutes, higher than six of the seven waits because the outlier 65 pulls it up. The median, 16, is resistant to the outlier and describes a typical wait.

n.0: Using every value is exactly why the mean is distorted here: the 65 drags it above six of the seven waits.
n.2: The range measures spread, not a typical value, and it is inflated by the outlier.
n.3: 14 appears only twice in seven values, so it says little about the center.

M.q: A graph of the total (cumulative) number of flu cases at a college shows 120 cases by the end of week 1, 210 by week 2, 270 by week 3, and 300 by week 4. A student says the graph shows the outbreak getting worse each week. Which statement about new cases per week is correct?
o: New cases fell each week, from 120 to 30
New cases stayed steady at about 75 per week
New cases rose each week, from 120 to 300
New cases peaked in week 4 at 300 cases
M.w: New cases each week are the differences between totals: 120, 210 - 120 = 90, 270 - 210 = 60, 300 - 270 = 30. A cumulative graph keeps rising even as new cases fall.

n.1: 300 / 4 = 75 is the mean per week; the actual weekly counts fell from 120 to 30.
n.2: 120 to 300 are running totals, not new cases each week.
n.3: 300 is the total after 4 weeks; only 30 of those cases were new in week 4.

M.q: A child has a fever of 102.2 °F. The pediatric chart records temperatures in degrees Celsius. What is the child's temperature in degrees Celsius? Round to the nearest tenth if necessary, and enter the number only.

tr.126.4: Subtracted 32 and then multiplied by 9/5 instead of 5/9.

M.q: A student is sorting triangles by type for a geometry project. Which set of side lengths forms a right triangle?
o: 8 cm, 15 cm, and 18 cm
6 cm, 9 cm, and 12 cm
7 cm, 24 cm, and 25 cm
5 cm, 12 cm, and 14 cm
M.w: Test a² + b² = c² with the longest side as c: 7² + 24² = 49 + 576 = 625 = 25². Only this set satisfies the Pythagorean theorem.

n.0: 8² + 15² = 289, which is 17², not 18² = 324.
n.3: 5² + 12² = 169, which is 13², not 14² = 196.

M.q: Solve for x: (x + 3)/5 = (x - 1)/3.
M.w: Cross-multiply: 3(x + 3) = 5(x - 1). Distribute: 3x + 9 = 5x - 5. Subtract 3x and add 5: 14 = 2x, so x = 7. Check: 10/5 = 2 and 6/3 = 2.

n.0: This cross-multiplies without distributing: 3x + 3 = 5x - 1 instead of 3(x + 3) = 5(x - 1).
n.2: Sign error in the last step: -2x = -14 gives a positive x.
n.3: This distributes on the left but not on the right: 3x + 9 = 5x - 1.

M.q: Gym A charges a $30 joining fee plus $25 per month. Gym B charges a $90 joining fee plus $19 per month. For the number of months at which the total costs of the two gyms are equal, what is that total cost?
M.w: Set the totals equal: 30 + 25m = 90 + 19m. Subtract 19m and 30 from both sides: 6m = 60, so m = 10 months. Total: 30 + 25(10) = $280. Check Gym B: 90 + 19(10) = $280.

n.0: This is Gym A's monthly charges for 10 months without the $30 joining fee.
n.1: This mixes the plans: Gym B's $90 fee with Gym A's $25 monthly rate for 10 months.
n.2: This adds the fees instead of subtracting them, giving 6m = 120 and m = 20 months, then 30 + 25(20) = $530.

M.q: A medication is ordered at 15 mg per kilogram of body weight per day, divided into 3 equal doses. A child weighs 44 pounds. Using 1 kg = 2.2 lb, how many milligrams should be given in each dose?
o: 300 mg
100 mg
660 mg
220 mg
M.w: Weight: 44 ÷ 2.2 = 20 kg. Daily dose: 15 × 20 = 300 mg. Each dose: 300 ÷ 3 = 100 mg.

n.0: This is the total daily dose; it must be divided into 3 equal doses.
n.2: This uses the weight in pounds and also gives a daily total, 44 × 15.
n.3: This uses the weight in pounds (44 × 15 ÷ 3) instead of converting to 20 kg first.

M.q: A roll of medical tape held 6 1/4 yards. A nurse used 2 3/4 yards while dressing wounds during a shift. How many yards of tape are left on the roll?
M.w: 1/4 is less than 3/4, so borrow 1 from 6: 6 1/4 = 5 5/4. Then 5 5/4 - 2 3/4 = 3 2/4 = 3 1/2 yards.

n.0: 4 1/2 subtracts 1/4 from 3/4 instead of borrowing (6 - 2 = 4 and 3/4 - 1/4 = 1/2).
n.1: 3 1/4 borrows 1 from 6 as 4/4 but drops the original 1/4 (5 4/4 - 2 3/4); the borrowed 4/4 and the 1/4 together make 5/4.
n.2: 5 comes from borrowing 1 as 10/4 instead of 4/4 (5 11/4 - 2 3/4 = 3 8/4 = 5).

M.q: Four tables each use the x-values 1, 2, 3, 4. Which set of y-values shows a linear relationship between x and y?
M.w: A relationship is linear when equal steps in x give equal differences in y. Here y rises by 3 each time (5, 8, 11, 14).

n.0: The differences are 2, 4, 6, which are not constant.
n.1: These are the squares of x; the differences are 3, 5, 7.
n.3: Each y doubles (a constant ratio), which is exponential; the differences are 2, 4, 8.

M.q: A clinic's goal is for each team to complete more than 0.7 of its training modules. Which of the following completion values are greater than 0.7? Select all that apply.

n.2: 9/13 ≈ 0.692, which is less than 0.7.
n.5: 7/10 = 0.7 exactly; it is equal to 0.7, not greater than it.

M.q: A medication refrigerator is set to 40°F. Its temperature t is acceptable when |t - 40| ≤ 3. Which recorded temperature is NOT acceptable?
M.w: |36.5 - 40| = |-3.5| = 3.5, which is greater than 3, so 36.5°F is not acceptable.

n.0: |43 - 40| = 3, and 3 ≤ 3 is true, so 43°F is acceptable.
n.2: |42.5 - 40| = 2.5, which is within 3 degrees.
n.3: |37 - 40| = 3, and 3 ≤ 3 is true, so 37°F is acceptable (the boundary is included).

M.q: A rectangular patient room measures 14 feet by 11 feet. New vinyl flooring costs $4.25 per square foot, including installation. What is the total cost to cover the entire floor of the room?

n.1: This takes half of the area, as if the floor were a triangle.
n.2: This uses 14 + 11 = 25, half the perimeter, instead of the area.
n.3: This uses the perimeter (2 × 14 + 2 × 11 = 50 ft) instead of the area.

M.q: A provider orders 60 mg of a liquid medication every 6 hours. The medication is supplied as 20 mg per 5 mL. How many milliliters will the patient receive in 24 hours?
o: 75 mL
15 mL
60 mL
360 mL
M.w: One dose: 60 ÷ 20 × 5 = 15 mL. Doses in 24 hours: 24 ÷ 6 = 4. Total: 4 × 15 = 60 mL.

n.0: This counts 5 doses by including both hour 0 and hour 24; every 6 hours gives 4 doses in a 24-hour day.
n.1: This is the volume for one dose; there are 24 ÷ 6 = 4 doses in 24 hours.
n.3: This multiplies one 15 mL dose by 24 as if a dose were given every hour.

M.q: A clinic can buy exam gloves in a box of 100 for $8.40 or in a case of 10 such boxes for $76.50. How much is saved per glove by buying the case instead of single boxes?
o: 0.75 cent
0.075 cent
75 cents
7.5 cents
M.w: Single box: $8.40 ÷ 100 = $0.084 per glove. Case: $76.50 ÷ 1,000 = $0.0765 per glove. Savings: 0.084 - 0.0765 = $0.0075 per glove, which is 0.75 cent.

n.1: Decimal slip: $0.0075 is 0.75 cent; this moves the decimal one place too far.
n.2: This is the savings per box of 100 gloves ($8.40 - $7.65), not per glove.
n.3: Decimal slip: $0.0075 is 0.75 of a cent, not 7.5 cents.

M.q: The minute hand of a wall clock in a nurses' station is 15 centimeters long. How far does the tip of the minute hand travel in 20 minutes? Use 3.14 for pi.
M.w: In 20 minutes the hand turns 20/60 = 1/3 of a circle. C = 2 × 3.14 × 15 = 94.2 cm. 94.2 ÷ 3 = 31.4 cm.

n.1: This takes 2/3 of the circumference; 20 minutes is 1/3 of an hour.
n.2: This takes 1/3 of πr (3.14 × 15) instead of 1/3 of 2πr.
n.3: This is the distance for a full hour, one complete circle.

M.q: A math teacher lists four everyday situations involving two related quantities. Which situation is an example of direct variation?
o: The balance on a $500 gift card after spending $25 per week
The time needed to drive 100 miles at different speeds
Total pay at $22 per hour, with no other pay
A taxi fare of $3 for pickup plus $2.50 per mile
M.w: Direct variation has the form y = kx: zero hours gives zero pay, and doubling the hours doubles the pay (pay = 22h).

n.0: Balance = 500 - 25w is a decreasing linear relationship, not y = kx.
n.1: Time = 100 / speed is inverse variation: doubling the speed halves the time.
n.3: Fare = 2.50m + 3 is linear, but the $3 starting fee means it does not pass through the origin, so it is not direct variation.

M.q: A pharmacy sells the same brand of vitamin gummies in four bottle sizes. Which bottle has the lowest price per gummy?
o: 24 gummies for $5.04
40 gummies for $8.20
16 gummies for $3.52
32 gummies for $6.08
M.w: Unit price = price ÷ quantity. $6.08 ÷ 32 = $0.19 per gummy, the lowest of $0.21, $0.19, $0.205, and $0.22.

n.0: $5.04 ÷ 24 = $0.21 per gummy, which is more than $0.19.
n.1: This is the largest bottle, but $8.20 ÷ 40 = $0.205 per gummy, which is more than $0.19.
n.2: This has the lowest total price, but $3.52 ÷ 16 = $0.22 per gummy, the highest unit price.

M.q: A decorative window is shaped like a semicircle with a straight bottom edge 4 feet long. A builder needs trim for the entire edge of the window, including the curved part and the straight bottom. How many feet of trim are needed? Use 3.14 for pi.
M.w: Curved part = 1/2 × πd = 1/2 × 3.14 × 4 = 6.28 ft. Add the straight edge (the diameter): 6.28 + 4 = 10.28 ft.

n.0: This adds the 4-foot straight edge to a full circle's circumference instead of half of it.
n.1: This is the circumference of a full circle (3.14 × 4).
n.3: This is the curved part by itself; the 4-foot straight edge must be added.

S.q: A bacterial culture contains 3.0 × 10⁴ cells per milliliter. A technician has 2.0 × 10³ mL of the culture. How many cells are in the full volume?
o: 6.0 × 10¹² cells
6.0 × 10¹ cells
5.0 × 10⁷ cells
6.0 × 10⁷ cells
S.w: To multiply in scientific notation, multiply the coefficients and add the exponents: (3.0 x 2.0) × 10⁽⁴⁺³⁾ = 6.0 × 10⁷ cells.

n.0: This multiplies the exponents (4 x 3 = 12); exponents are added when multiplying.
n.1: This subtracts the exponents (4 - 3), the rule for division, not multiplication.
n.2: This adds the coefficients (3.0 + 2.0); coefficients are multiplied.

S.q: Chlorine has atomic number 17. In a neutral chlorine atom, how many electrons occupy the outermost (third) electron shell? Enter your answer as a whole number.

tr.1: Counted the electrons chlorine needs to gain, not the electrons it has.
tr.8: Assumed the outer shell is a full octet; chlorine is one electron short of 8.
tr.17: Gave the total number of electrons, not the outer-shell count.

S.w: Fill shells from the inside: first shell 2, second shell 8, which uses 10 electrons. The remaining 17 - 2 - 8 = 7 electrons are in the third shell (arrangement 2, 8, 7), matching chlorine's place in group 17.

S.q: The rate of a human enzyme-catalyzed reaction rises as the temperature increases from 20 °C to 37 °C, then drops sharply at 50 °C. What best explains the drop?
o: The heat raises the activation energy of the reaction.
The enzyme denatures, and its active site loses its shape.
The enzyme is used up as it converts more of the substrate.
The heat breaks the peptide bonds in the enzyme's chain.
S.w: Above its optimum (about 37 °C for most human enzymes) the enzyme denatures: its folding is disrupted, the active site changes shape, and the substrate no longer fits.

n.0: Enzymes work by lowering activation energy. The drop is due to loss of enzyme shape, not a change in activation energy.
n.2: Enzymes are catalysts and are not consumed by the reactions they speed up.
n.3: Denaturation disrupts folding; the peptide bonds of the primary sequence stay intact.

S.q: The pancreas has an exocrine part and an endocrine part. Which of these products is released through ducts into the duodenum rather than into the blood?
o: Somatostatin made by delta cells
Insulin made by beta cells
Glucagon made by alpha cells
Trypsinogen made by acinar cells
S.w: Acinar cells of the exocrine pancreas make pancreatic juice, including trypsinogen, which travels through ducts to the duodenum. Islet hormones enter the blood.

n.0: Somatostatin is an islet hormone that acts on other islet cells; it is not part of pancreatic juice.
n.1: Insulin is an endocrine hormone from the islets and enters the blood, not a duct.
n.2: Glucagon is an islet hormone secreted into the blood to raise blood glucose.

S.q: Tendons attach skeletal muscles to bones and must resist strong pulling forces in one direction. Which tissue forms tendons?
o: Dense irregular connective tissue
Loose areolar connective tissue
Dense regular connective tissue
Skeletal muscle tissue
S.w: Tendons and ligaments are dense regular connective tissue: tightly packed collagen fibers run parallel to one another, resisting strong pull in one direction.
