n.0: Dense irregular connective tissue has collagen fibers running in many directions, suited to pull from several directions (as in the dermis), not the parallel fibers of a tendon.
n.1: Areolar tissue is loose connective tissue with a loose, open arrangement of fibers; it does not withstand strong one-direction pull.
n.3: Skeletal muscle generates the pull; the tendon that transmits it to bone is connective tissue.

S.q: A patient's chart notes a rash in the popliteal region and on the plantar surface of the same leg. Which two areas are affected?
o: The front of the thigh and the sole of the foot
The front of the knee and the sole of the foot
The back of the knee and the sole of the foot
The back of the knee and the top of the foot
S.w: Two regional terms: popliteal means the back of the knee, and plantar means the sole of the foot.

n.0: The front of the thigh is part of the femoral region; popliteal is the back of the knee.
n.1: The front of the knee is the patellar region; popliteal is the back of the knee.
n.3: Popliteal is right, but plantar is the sole, not the top of the foot.

S.q: Several weeks after a kidney transplant, the recipient's immune system begins attacking the donor organ. Which cells directly kill the transplanted kidney cells?
o: Helper (CD4) T cells
Antibody-secreting plasma cells
Cytotoxic (CD8) T cells
Regulatory T cells
S.w: Cytotoxic (CD8) T cells of cell-mediated immunity directly kill virus-infected cells, cancer cells and transplanted cells.

n.0: Helper T cells coordinate the attack through cytokines but do not kill the cells themselves.
n.1: Plasma cells secrete antibodies; they do not make direct cell-to-cell kills.
n.3: Regulatory T cells suppress immune responses; they would dampen rejection rather than carry it out.

S.q: Each eye has a small blind spot where the optic nerve leaves the retina at the optic disc. Why does no image form at this point?
o: It contains no photoreceptors
It contains rods but no cones
It lies in front of the lens
It is covered by the opaque sclera
S.w: The optic disc has no photoreceptors (no rods or cones), so light falling on it cannot be detected.

n.1: A region with rods would still detect light in black and white; the optic disc has neither rods nor cones.
n.2: The optic disc is part of the retina at the back of the eye, behind the lens.
n.3: The sclera is the white outer layer of the eyeball; it does not cover the inner surface of the retina.

S.q: Pepsin digests protein in the stomach, where the pH is about 2. If pepsin passes into the small intestine, where the pH is about 8, what will most likely happen to its activity?
o: It will fall, since pH 8 is far from pepsin's optimum.
It will stay the same, since pH does not affect enzymes.
It will rise, since trypsin activates pepsin at pH 8.
It will rise, since enzymes work faster in basic solutions.
S.w: Each enzyme has an optimum pH. Pepsin works best near pH 2, so at pH 8 its shape changes and activity falls. Trypsin, with an optimum near pH 8, works in the small intestine.

n.1: pH strongly affects enzyme shape and activity.
n.2: Trypsin is a separate protein-digesting enzyme with its own optimum; it does not boost pepsin.
n.3: Enzymes do not all work faster in basic conditions; each has its own optimum, and pepsin's is acidic.

S.q: Stirring a cup of iced tea makes the added sugar dissolve faster. Which statement correctly describes what stirring changes?
o: The temperature of the tea, which raises the solubility
The solubility of sugar, so more sugar can dissolve in total
The speed of dissolving, but not the solubility of sugar
Both the solubility of sugar and the speed of dissolving
S.w: Stirring brings fresh solvent into contact with the solute, increasing the rate of dissolving. Solubility, the maximum amount that can dissolve, depends on temperature (and pressure for gases), not on stirring.

n.0: Stirring does not noticeably change the temperature of the tea, so it does not change solubility.
n.1: Stirring affects how fast sugar dissolves, not the total amount that can dissolve.
n.3: Stirring changes the rate only; solubility at a given temperature is fixed.

S.q: In a trial of a blood-pressure drug, neither the patients nor the nurses who take the readings know which patients receive the drug and which receive a placebo. Which term describes this design feature?
o: Observational study
Double-blind
Random sampling
Single-blind
S.w: In a double-blind study, neither the subjects nor the researchers who measure outcomes know group assignments, which reduces bias from both expectations.

n.0: An observational study assigns no treatment; this trial gives a drug or placebo.
n.2: Random sampling is how participants are chosen so the sample represents the population; it does not hide group assignments.
n.3: Single-blind means the subjects do not know their group, but the researchers do.

S.q: A runner moves to a high-altitude city where the air holds less oxygen, and over several weeks her red blood cell count rises. Which organ releases the hormone responsible?
o: The liver, which releases erythropoietin
Red bone marrow, which releases erythropoietin
The spleen, which releases erythropoietin
The kidneys, which release erythropoietin
S.w: Step 1: low blood oxygen is sensed by the kidneys. Step 2: the kidneys release erythropoietin (EPO), which stimulates red bone marrow to make more red blood cells.

n.0: The liver makes plasma proteins such as albumin; in adults, EPO comes from the kidneys.
n.1: Red bone marrow responds to EPO by making RBCs; it does not secrete the hormone.
n.2: The spleen removes old red blood cells; it does not release EPO.

S.q: A drug overdose depresses the brain region containing the vital centers that set heart rate, breathing rhythm and blood pressure. Which region is this?
o: Primary motor cortex
Hypothalamus
Cerebellum
Medulla oblongata
S.w: The medulla oblongata of the brainstem contains the vital centers for heart rate, breathing rhythm and blood pressure, as well as reflexes such as coughing and swallowing.

n.0: The primary motor cortex in the frontal lobe controls voluntary movement, not heart rate or breathing rhythm.
n.1: The hypothalamus regulates body temperature, hunger, thirst and water balance; the vital centers are in the medulla oblongata.
n.2: The cerebellum coordinates movement, balance and posture; it does not contain the vital centers.

S.q: A sealed syringe of air is kept at constant temperature while a student changes the pressure. Data: 100 kPa, 60 mL; 200 kPa, 30 mL; 300 kPa, 20 mL. Which relationship do the data show?
o: Direct: volume falls as pressure rises
No relationship: the values vary randomly
Direct: volume rises as pressure rises
Inverse: volume falls as pressure rises
S.w: When one variable increases as the other decreases, the relationship is inverse. Doubling the pressure halves the volume (100 kPa x 60 mL = 200 kPa x 30 mL = 300 kPa x 20 mL), the pattern of gas pressure and volume at constant temperature.

n.0: The trend is described correctly, but one variable falling as the other rises is an inverse relationship, not a direct one.
n.1: The values change in a steady, predictable pattern (pressure x volume stays constant), not randomly.
n.2: The volume does not rise; it drops from 60 mL to 20 mL as pressure increases.

S.q: Pancreatic juice contains enzymes for each major class of nutrient. Which enzyme in pancreatic juice breaks down the DNA and RNA found in food?
o: Chymotrypsin
Maltase
Peptidase
Nuclease
S.w: Pancreatic nucleases digest nucleic acids into nucleotides, which are broken into sugars, bases and phosphate and absorbed into the blood.

n.0: Chymotrypsin is a pancreatic enzyme, but it digests proteins.
n.1: Maltase is a brush-border enzyme that splits the sugar maltose.
n.2: Peptidases are brush-border enzymes that finish protein digestion.

S.q: Analysis of a sample of double-stranded DNA shows that 22% of its bases are thymine. What percentage of its bases are guanine? Enter your answer as a whole-number percent.

tr.22: assumed guanine equals thymine instead of adenine
tr.56: found G + C but did not split it between G and C
tr.78: subtracted thymine once from 100 and stopped

S.w: Step 1: A = T, so A is also 22%, and A + T = 44%. Step 2: G + C = 100% - 44% = 56%. Step 3: G = C, so G = 56% / 2 = 28%.

S.q: In a class discussion about how science works, a student asks how a scientific law differs from a scientific theory. Which statement gives the correct distinction?
o: A law explains why an event happens; a theory describes the pattern.
A theory becomes a law once enough experiments have proven it correct.
A theory is an educated guess that scientists have not yet tested.
A law describes what consistently happens; a theory explains why.
S.w: A law describes a consistent pattern, often mathematically (conservation of mass), without explaining it. A theory is a broad, well-tested explanation of many observations (cell theory). They do different jobs, so theories do not turn into laws.

n.0: This swaps the roles: laws describe, and theories explain.
n.1: Theories do not graduate into laws; a well-supported theory stays a theory because it explains rather than describes.
n.2: That describes a hypothesis; a theory is supported by extensive, repeated testing.

S.q: During fetal development, most bones form by replacing a hyaline cartilage model. Which bone instead forms directly within a fibrous membrane by intramembranous ossification?
o: Humerus
Vertebra
Femur
Clavicle
S.w: Intramembranous ossification builds bone directly in a fibrous membrane: the flat bones of the skull, the clavicles and some facial bones. Long bones and vertebrae form by endochondral ossification, replacing a hyaline cartilage model.

n.0: The humerus is a long bone that forms by endochondral ossification from a cartilage model.
n.1: Vertebrae are irregular bones that form by endochondral ossification from cartilage models.
n.2: The femur is a long bone that forms by endochondral ossification from a cartilage model.

S.q: A person performs one slow biceps curl: raising a dumbbell, holding it still at mid-height for five seconds, then lowering it slowly. Which statements about the biceps brachii are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Raising the dumbbell is a concentric contraction
Lowering it slowly is an isometric contraction
Holding it still is an isometric contraction
Lowering it slowly is an eccentric contraction
Holding it still is a concentric contraction
S.w: Isotonic contractions change muscle length: concentric when the muscle shortens (lifting) and eccentric when it lengthens under load (lowering). Isometric contractions build tension with no change in length (holding still).

n.1: While lowering, the biceps lengthens under load, which is eccentric; isometric means no change in length.
n.4: While holding still, the biceps keeps the same length, which is isometric; concentric means the muscle shortens.

S.q: A segment of the DNA template strand reads 3'-TAC-5'. Which mRNA codon is transcribed from it, and what is that codon's role?
o: UAC, copied directly from the template
AUG, the start codon for methionine
AUG, a stop codon that ends translation
ATG, a codon read at the ribosome
S.w: Base pairing gives T->A, A->U, C->G, so 3'-TAC-5' is transcribed into 5'-AUG-3'. AUG is the start codon and codes for methionine.

n.0: Transcription makes a complementary copy, not an identical one; UAC is the matching tRNA anticodon.
n.2: AUG is the start codon. The stop codons are UAA, UAG and UGA.
n.3: mRNA contains uracil, not thymine, so the codon cannot be ATG.

S.q: LDL particles carrying cholesterol bind to specific proteins on the surface of a liver cell, and the membrane then folds inward to bring them in. Which process is this?
o: Phagocytosis of a large particle
Exocytosis by a secretory vesicle
Receptor-mediated endocytosis
Facilitated diffusion via a carrier
S.w: Binding of a specific substance to surface receptors followed by inward folding of the membrane into a vesicle is receptor-mediated endocytosis, the route for cholesterol (LDL).

n.0: Phagocytosis is endocytosis of large particles such as bacteria by cells such as neutrophils, not receptor-specific uptake of LDL.
n.1: Exocytosis releases material from the cell; this material is entering.
n.3: Facilitated diffusion moves single molecules through channels or carriers, without forming vesicles.

S.q: Fresh milk scatters a beam of light shone through it, and its tiny dispersed particles do not settle out even after the milk stands for hours. How is milk best classified?
o: A solution
A suspension
A compound
A colloid
S.w: A colloid is a mixture whose dispersed particles are larger than in a solution but do not settle; they scatter light (the Tyndall effect). Milk, fog and gelatin are colloids.

n.0: Solution particles are too small to scatter a light beam; a true solution looks clear.
n.1: Suspension particles are large enough to settle out on standing and can be filtered.
n.2: Milk is a mixture of many substances in variable proportions, not a single compound with a fixed ratio.

S.q: Pasta takes longer to cook in boiling water in Denver, Colorado (elevation about 5,280 feet) than in Miami, Florida, near sea level. What explains this difference?
o: Colder air at high altitude removes heat from the pot more quickly
Thinner air holds less oxygen, which lowers water's boiling point
Lower air pressure at high altitude lowers water's boiling point
Higher air pressure at high altitude slows the escape of molecules
S.w: A liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the surrounding pressure. At high altitude, air pressure is lower, so water boils at a lower temperature (below 100 °C). The boiling water is cooler, so food cooks more slowly.

n.0: Once water boils, its temperature is set by the boiling point, not by the outside air temperature.
n.1: The boiling point is lower at altitude, but the cause is lower air pressure; the oxygen content of the air does not set the boiling point of water.
n.3: Air pressure is lower, not higher, at high altitude. Higher pressure (as in a pressure cooker) raises the boiling point.

S.q: Years of smoking destroy many of the cilia that line a patient's bronchi. Which normal airway function is most directly impaired?
o: Sweeping mucus and trapped particles up toward the pharynx
Producing mucus from goblet cells to trap inhaled dust
Warming and humidifying air as it passes over the conchae
Secreting surfactant to keep the alveoli from collapsing
S.w: Cilia on the airway epithelium beat to move the mucus sheet, with its trapped particles, up toward the pharynx (the mucociliary escalator). Without cilia, mucus pools and is cleared by coughing.

n.1: Mucus is made by goblet cells, not cilia, so mucus is still produced; it is moving it that fails.
n.2: Warming and humidifying occur mainly in the nasal cavity, over the vascular mucosa of the conchae, not by bronchial cilia.
n.3: Surfactant is secreted by type II alveolar cells, which have no cilia.

S.q: A cell-culture incubator's display reads 98.6 °F. A data logger in the same lab records temperature in kelvins. Enter the incubator temperature in kelvins, rounded to the nearest whole number.

tr.37: Converted to Celsius (37 °C) but stopped before adding 273.
tr.236: Converted to Celsius and then subtracted it from 273 instead of adding.
tr.372: Added 273 directly to the Fahrenheit reading (98.6 + 273 = 371.6) without converting to Celsius first.

S.q: In a sample of testicular tissue, 25 primary spermatocytes each complete both meiotic divisions normally. How many spermatids are produced in total? Enter a whole number.

tr.25: One gamete per cell, as in oogenesis.
tr.50: Counting meiosis I only (2 secondary spermatocytes per primary spermatocyte).

S.w: Each primary spermatocyte goes through meiosis I (giving 2 secondary spermatocytes) and meiosis II (giving 4 haploid spermatids). Unlike oogenesis, which yields 1 ovum plus polar bodies, no cells are lost as polar bodies. 25 x 4 = 100 spermatids.

S.q: Reaction rate at five substrate concentrations, with enzyme amount held constant: 1 mM, 10; 2 mM, 18; 4 mM, 28; 8 mM, 33; 16 mM, 34 (rate in units per minute). What is the best prediction for the rate at 32 mM?
o: About 34, since the rate has nearly leveled off
About 44, since the rate keeps rising by a steady amount
About 68, since doubling substrate doubles the rate
About 20, since the rate falls once past an optimum
S.w: The rate rises quickly and then plateaus: from 8 to 16 mM it gains only 1 unit because the enzyme molecules are nearly saturated. Doubling the substrate again should leave the rate close to 34.

n.1: The increases shrink (8, 10, 5, 1), so the rate is leveling off, not rising steadily.
n.2: Doubling 16 mM to 32 mM does not double the rate; going from 8 to 16 mM added only 1 unit.
n.3: A rise-then-fall curve fits enzyme activity against temperature or pH, not against substrate concentration.

S.q: Which glands secrete an oily substance, usually into hair follicles, that softens skin and hair, slows water loss and helps inhibit bacterial growth?
o: Sebaceous glands
Ceruminous glands
Apocrine sweat glands
Eccrine sweat glands
S.w: Sebaceous (oil) glands secrete sebum, usually into hair follicles. Sebum lubricates and softens skin and hair, slows water loss and is antibacterial. They are absent from the palms and soles.

n.1: Ceruminous glands are modified sweat glands that produce earwax in the ear canal.
n.2: Apocrine glands also open into hair follicles, but they secrete a thicker sweat, not oily sebum.
n.3: Eccrine glands open onto the skin surface through pores and secrete watery sweat.

S.q: A class measures how fast an enzyme breaks down hydrogen peroxide at 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60 °C. How should the axes of their graph be labeled?
o: Enzyme activity on the x-axis; temperature on the y-axis
Time on the x-axis; temperature on the y-axis
Time on the x-axis; enzyme activity on the y-axis
Temperature on the x-axis; enzyme activity on the y-axis
S.w: The independent variable (temperature, which the class sets) goes on the x-axis, and the dependent variable (enzyme activity, which is measured) goes on the y-axis.

n.0: This places the dependent variable on the x-axis; it belongs on the y-axis.
n.1: This leaves the dependent variable, enzyme activity, off the graph.
n.2: Time is not the variable the class changed; temperature is the independent variable here.

S.q: A hypothesis states that every strain of a bacterium is killed by a certain antibiotic. Forty lab tests support it. Then a replicated study by another lab finds a strain that survives the antibiotic. What is the correct conclusion?
o: The hypothesis is refuted and must be revised.
The new strain should be dropped as an outlier.
The hypothesis stands, since 40 tests outweigh one.
The hypothesis is proven for the strains tested.
S.w: Supporting evidence never proves a general claim, but one well-replicated contradicting result can refute it. The claim about every strain must be revised.

n.1: A replicated result is not an outlier; discarding inconvenient data biases the conclusion.
n.2: Science does not decide by vote; one replicated counterexample defeats a claim about every strain.
n.3: Data support hypotheses but do not prove them, and the claim was about all strains, not some.

S.q: A textbook diagram labels the plasma membrane of an animal cell as a fluid mosaic. Which description of the membrane is consistent with this model?
o: A rigid layer of cellulose that small solutes pass through
A phospholipid bilayer that ions cross with no protein help
A double layer of proteins coated with phospholipid heads
A phospholipid bilayer with proteins that drift within it
S.w: The fluid mosaic model describes a phospholipid bilayer in which proteins, cholesterol (in animal cells) and glycoproteins are embedded and can move laterally, forming a selectively permeable barrier.

n.0: A cellulose layer describes a plant cell wall, which lies outside the plasma membrane.
n.1: Ions are charged and cannot easily cross the hydrophobic interior; they need channel or carrier proteins.
n.2: The membrane's framework is a phospholipid bilayer, with proteins embedded in it, not a protein double layer.

S.q: A man with red-green color blindness, an X-linked recessive trait, has children with a woman who carries no color-blindness allele. Which outcome is expected?
o: Half of the sons are color-blind and half of the daughters are carriers.
All of the daughters are carriers and none of the sons are color-blind.
Half of the daughters are color-blind and none of the sons are affected.
All of the sons are color-blind and none of the daughters are carriers.
S.w: Step 1: the father passes his X (with the allele) to every daughter and his Y to every son. Step 2: daughters get a normal X from the mother, so all are carriers; sons get the mother's normal X, so none are affected.

n.0: This is the pattern for a carrier mother and a normal father, not an affected father and a noncarrier mother.
n.2: Each daughter gets a normal X from her mother, which masks the recessive allele, so she is a carrier, not affected.
n.3: Sons receive the father's Y, not his X, so they cannot inherit his X-linked allele.

S.q: A patient who spends almost no time outdoors develops low blood calcium. Which sequence best describes the skin's normal role in calcium absorption from the intestine?
o: Melanocytes secrete vitamin D3 after UVB exposure; the kidneys then activate it
UVB converts a cholesterol derivative directly into active calcitriol in skin
Sebaceous glands secrete vitamin D3 in sebum; the liver then activates it
UVB makes vitamin D3 from a cholesterol derivative; liver and kidneys activate it
S.w: Step 1: in the skin, UVB converts a cholesterol derivative to vitamin D3, an inactive precursor. Step 2: the liver and kidneys convert it to active calcitriol, which increases calcium absorption from the gut. Little sun means little D3 and poorer Ca²⁺ absorption.

n.0: Melanocytes make melanin, which absorbs UV; vitamin D3 forms from a cholesterol derivative in the skin, and the liver also takes part in activation.
n.1: The skin makes only the precursor; activation to calcitriol takes place in the liver and kidneys.
n.2: Sebaceous glands secrete sebum to lubricate skin; vitamin D3 forms from a cholesterol derivative, and the kidneys also take part in activation.

S.q: A breeder owns a black guinea pig, where black (B) is dominant over white (b), and wants to know whether it is BB or Bb. Which cross would best answer this question?
o: Cross it with a heterozygous black (Bb) guinea pig.
Cross it with a white (bb) guinea pig.
Cross it with another black guinea pig of unknown genotype.
Cross it with a homozygous black (BB) guinea pig.
S.w: A test cross pairs the unknown dominant-phenotype individual with a homozygous recessive (bb). Any white offspring prove the unknown parent carries b, so it is Bb.

n.0: A Bb partner passes on b only half the time, so white pups appear less often (1/4 instead of 1/2 if the unknown is Bb). It is a weaker test than crossing with bb.
n.2: An unknown partner adds a second unknown, so the results cannot be interpreted.
n.3: Every offspring of a BB parent shows black whatever the other parent is, so the cross cannot reveal a hidden b allele.

S.q: Before giving an injection, a nurse cleans the patient's skin with an alcohol-based solution to reduce the number of microbes. What is this practice called?
o: Sterilization
Antisepsis
Disinfection
Pasteurization
S.w: Antisepsis reduces microbes on living tissue such as skin. Disinfection is for objects and surfaces.

n.0: Sterilization kills all microbes including endospores (as in an autoclave) and is not done on skin.
n.2: Disinfection reduces pathogens on objects and surfaces, not on living tissue.
n.3: Pasteurization is gentle heating of foods such as milk, not skin preparation.

S.q: A healthy adult's spirometry shows a tidal volume of 500 mL, an inspiratory reserve volume of 3,000 mL, an expiratory reserve volume of 1,100 mL and a residual volume of 1,200 mL. What is the vital capacity? Enter your answer in milliliters as a whole number.

tr.3500: Added only tidal volume and inspiratory reserve volume (inspiratory capacity).
tr.5800: Added the residual volume as well; that gives total lung capacity.

S.w: Vital capacity = tidal volume + inspiratory reserve volume + expiratory reserve volume = 500 + 3,000 + 1,100 = 4,600 mL. Residual volume is not included because it cannot be exhaled.

S.q: Place these attractive forces in order of strength, starting with the weakest.
o: London dispersion forces
Covalent bonds
Hydrogen bonds
Dipole-dipole attractions
S.w: Intermolecular forces rank London dispersion < dipole-dipole < hydrogen bonds. All three are weaker than the covalent bonds that hold atoms together within a molecule.

S.q: A cell-culture protocol calls for 0.075 L of buffer solution. The graduated cylinder on the bench is marked in milliliters. Enter the volume to measure, in milliliters, as a whole number.

tr.750: Moved the decimal point four places.
tr.7.5: Moved the decimal point only two places (multiplied by 100, the centi factor).
tr.0.000075: Divided by 1,000 instead of multiplying when going from a larger to a smaller unit.

S.w: 1 L = 1,000 mL. Converting from a larger unit (liters) to a smaller unit (milliliters) means multiplying: 0.075 x 1,000 = 75 mL. Move the decimal point three places to the right.

S.q: Atrial repolarization does not appear as a separate wave on a normal ECG. Why?
o: It occurs during the QRS complex and is hidden by it
It occurs during the T wave and is hidden by it
It occurs after the T wave and is too small to record
It occurs during the P wave and is hidden by it
S.w: The atria repolarize at about the same time the ventricles depolarize, so the small atrial repolarization signal is masked by the much larger QRS complex.

n.1: The T wave is ventricular repolarization, which happens later, while the atria are already at rest.
n.2: After the T wave the whole heart is at rest; the atria repolarized much earlier.
n.3: The P wave is atrial depolarization; repolarization cannot occur at the same moment.

S.q: A 45-year-old patient with obesity has high blood glucose even though his pancreas still produces insulin. Which description best fits his condition?
o: Type 1 diabetes mellitus caused by beta-cell destruction
Type 2 diabetes mellitus caused by insulin resistance
Diabetes insipidus caused by a lack of ADH
Type 1 diabetes mellitus caused by insulin resistance
S.w: Type 2 diabetes mellitus is mainly insulin resistance (with a relative deficiency) and is linked to obesity and inactivity; insulin is still produced.

n.0: Beta-cell destruction leaves no insulin, but this patient still produces insulin.
n.2: Diabetes insipidus is an ADH problem causing dilute urine; it does not raise blood glucose.
n.3: Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune destruction of beta cells; insulin resistance defines type 2.

S.q: When a sample containing sodium is held in a flame, the flame turns a bright yellow-orange. Which process in the sodium atoms produces this colored light?
o: Electrons absorbing heat and moving to higher energy levels
Excited electrons falling back to lower energy levels
Protons leaving the nucleus as the atoms are strongly heated
Sodium atoms combining with oxygen to form a new compound
S.w: Heat excites electrons to higher energy levels. When they fall back to lower levels, they emit the extra energy as light of specific colors, which is why each element has a characteristic flame color and emission spectrum.

n.0: Absorbing energy raises electrons to higher levels, but light is given off when they drop back down, not as they move up.
n.2: Protons do not leave the nucleus in a flame; flame color comes from electron transitions.
n.3: Flame color is a property of the element's electrons, not of a combustion product; sodium compounds give the same color.

S.q: Ammonia is made by the reaction N₂ + 3 H₂ ⇌ 2 NH₃. While the mixture is at equilibrium, more N₂ gas is pumped into the container. How does the system respond?
o: It shifts right, forming more NH₃
It stays put, because the rates were equal
It shifts left, forming more N₂
It shifts left, forming more H₂
S.w: Le Chatelier's principle: a system at equilibrium shifts to counteract a stress. Adding a reactant (N₂) is relieved by using some of it up, so the equilibrium shifts right, toward the product, forming more NH₃.

n.1: Adding N₂ speeds the forward reaction, so the rates are no longer equal until the system shifts and reaches a new equilibrium.
n.2: The system responds by consuming some of the added N₂, not by making more of it.
n.3: Shifting left would produce more reactants and increase the stress; adding a reactant drives the reaction toward products.

S.q: A tissue sample shows branched, striated cells, each with one central nucleus, joined end to end by intercalated discs. From which location was the sample most likely taken?
o: Wall of the stomach
Wall of a large artery
Biceps brachii of the arm
Wall of the heart
S.w: Branched, striated cells with usually one nucleus, joined by intercalated discs (gap junctions plus desmosomes), are cardiac muscle, found only in the heart wall.

n.0: The stomach wall is smooth muscle: spindle-shaped, nonstriated cells without intercalated discs.
n.1: Artery walls contain smooth muscle, which is nonstriated and lacks intercalated discs.
n.2: The biceps brachii is skeletal muscle: long, cylindrical, multinucleated fibers without intercalated discs.

S.q: Starting from anatomical position, a patient turns the forearm so that the palm faces backward, with the radius crossing over the ulna. What is this movement called?
o: Circumduction
Inversion
Supination
Pronation
S.w: Pronation turns the palm to face posteriorly (or downward) as the radius crosses over the ulna. Supination is the reverse, returning the palm to face anteriorly as in anatomical position.

n.0: Circumduction is a cone-shaped movement of a limb, as at the shoulder or hip.
n.1: Inversion turns the sole of the foot inward; it is a foot movement.
n.2: Supination turns the palm forward or upward; in anatomical position the forearm is already supinated.

S.q: A lab reports that a patient's arterial blood has a pH of 7.32. How should this value be classified?
o: Alkalosis, because it is above the neutral pH of 7
Acidosis, because it is below the normal range of 7.35-7.45
Normal, because blood is slightly acidic at about 7.3
Normal, because it is within 0.5 of the neutral pH of 7
S.w: Normal blood pH is 7.35-7.45, which is slightly basic. A pH below 7.35 is acidosis and a pH above 7.45 is alkalosis, so 7.32 is acidosis even though it is above 7.

n.0: Blood is judged against its normal range, not against neutral 7; 7.32 is below that range, which is acidosis.
n.2: Normal blood is slightly basic (7.35-7.45), not slightly acidic, and 7.32 falls below the normal range.
n.3: The healthy range is narrow (7.35-7.45); being near 7 is not the standard for blood.

S.q: A drop in blood pressure triggers the release of renin, the first step in a chain that raises blood pressure again. Which statement about renin is correct?
o: It is an enzyme in the lungs that forms angiotensin II
It is an enzyme from juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney
It is a hormone secreted by the adrenal cortex
It is a hormone from the heart atria that lowers pressure
S.w: Renin is an enzyme released by juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney when blood pressure or sodium is low. It converts angiotensinogen into angiotensin I.

n.0: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), found mostly in the lungs, forms angiotensin II; renin acts earlier.
n.2: The adrenal cortex releases aldosterone later in the pathway; renin comes from the kidney.
n.3: ANP from the atria lowers blood pressure; renin is part of the system that raises it.

S.q: A study reporting that a sports drink improves endurance was paid for by the company that makes the drink. Eight cyclists were randomly assigned to the drink or a look-alike placebo, and the testers did not know who drank which. Which concerns are most relevant when evaluating this study?
o: Conflict of interest and no placebo group
No blinding and a conflict of interest
Conflict of interest and a small sample
No random assignment and a small sample
S.w: When evaluating a claim, ask whether the source is unbiased and the sample is large enough. Funding from the drink's maker is a conflict of interest, and 8 participants is easily skewed by chance. The design itself used random assignment, a placebo and blinding.

n.0: The other cyclists drank a look-alike placebo, so the study did have a placebo control.
n.1: The testers did not know who drank which, so the measurements were blinded; only the conflict of interest applies.
n.3: The cyclists were randomly assigned to groups, so assignment bias is not the concern; only the small sample is.

S.q: Six primary oocytes and six primary spermatocytes complete meiosis normally, and each oocyte is fertilized so that meiosis II finishes. How many ova and how many sperm result in total?
o: 6 ova and 24 sperm
6 ova and 12 sperm
24 ova and 24 sperm
12 ova and 24 sperm
S.w: Two steps. (1) Oogenesis divides the cytoplasm unequally, so each primary oocyte yields 1 ovum plus polar bodies: 6 x 1 = 6 ova. (2) Spermatogenesis yields 4 sperm per primary spermatocyte: 6 x 4 = 24 sperm.

n.1: This counts 2 sperm per spermatocyte, which stops after meiosis I; meiosis II gives 4 per spermatocyte.
n.2: This treats oogenesis like spermatogenesis; polar bodies are not functional ova, so each oocyte gives 1 ovum.
n.3: This counts the first polar body as a second ovum; polar bodies degenerate and are not ova.

S.q: A sample of bacteria from a patient's wound is Gram stained and appears purple under the microscope. What does this result indicate about the bacteria?
o: Gram-negative, with an outer lipid membrane
Gram-negative, with a thick peptidoglycan wall
Gram-positive, with a thin wall and outer membrane
Gram-positive, with a thick peptidoglycan wall
S.w: Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan wall that holds the purple (violet) stain. Gram-negative bacteria have a thin wall plus an outer membrane and stain pink or red.

n.0: An outer membrane is the Gram-negative feature, and those bacteria stain pink, not purple.
n.1: Gram-negative bacteria stain pink and have a thin peptidoglycan layer, not a thick one.
n.2: A thin wall with an outer membrane is the Gram-negative structure, which does not stain purple.

S.q: A chemistry teacher asks which pair of elements would most likely combine to form an ionic compound. Which pair should the students choose?
o: Copper and zinc
Potassium and bromine
Phosphorus and chlorine
Nitrogen and oxygen
S.w: Ionic bonds form between a metal and a nonmetal with a large electronegativity difference. Potassium (an alkali metal) readily loses an electron to bromine (a halogen), forming KBr.

n.0: Copper and zinc are both metals; together they form an alloy (brass) held by metallic bonding.
n.2: Phosphorus and chlorine are both nonmetals and form covalent bonds, as in PCl₃.
n.3: Nitrogen and oxygen are both nonmetals, so they share electrons in covalent bonds.

E.q: A writer wants to turn "The doctor reviewed the X-ray, and she ordered a CT scan" into a simple sentence without changing its meaning. Which revision does this correctly?
o: After the doctor reviewed the X-ray, she ordered a CT scan.
The doctor, who reviewed the X-ray, ordered a CT scan.
The doctor reviewed the X-ray; she ordered a CT scan.
The doctor reviewed the X-ray and ordered a CT scan.
E.w: Removing the second subject (she) leaves one subject with a compound predicate (reviewed ... and ordered): one independent clause, a simple sentence.

n.0: "After the doctor reviewed the X-ray" is a dependent clause, so the result is complex.
n.1: "Who reviewed the X-ray" is a dependent relative clause, so the result is complex.
n.2: A semicolon joining two independent clauses still makes a compound sentence.

E.q: Read the sentence: "After the meeting, the staff ate lunch in the break room." What is the word group "After the meeting"?
o: An appositive phrase
An independent clause
A prepositional phrase
A dependent clause
E.w: "After" works here as a preposition with the object "the meeting". There is no verb, so the group is a phrase, not a clause.

n.0: An appositive renames a nearby noun; "After the meeting" tells when, it does not rename anything.
n.1: An independent clause needs a subject and verb and must express a complete thought.
n.3: A dependent clause needs a subject and a verb (for example, "After the meeting ended"); this group has no verb.

E.q: A patient was diagnosed with hemiplegia and began a rehabilitation program with a physical therapist three times a week. Based on its word parts, what does hemiplegia mean?
o: Paralysis on one side of the body
Paralysis caused by a brain bleed
Paralysis affecting both of the legs
Paralysis of all four of the limbs
E.w: hemi- means half and -plegia means paralysis, so hemiplegia is paralysis of one half (one side) of the body.

n.1: hemi- (half) is not hem/o (blood); the word says nothing about bleeding.
n.2: Paralysis of both legs is paraplegia; hemi- refers to one side, not both legs.
n.3: Paralysis of all four limbs is quadriplegia; quadri- means four.

E.q: A lab manager is reviewing safety notes before they are posted. Which sentence has a pronoun that agrees with its antecedent in number and person?
o: The lab and the pharmacy will extend its hours in December.
If a student wants to pass, you have to practice every day.
All of the incubators must have its filters changed every month.
Each of the vials must be inspected for cracks before it is used.
E.w: "Each" is singular, and a vial is a thing, so the singular pronoun "it" agrees in number and person.

n.0: Two antecedents joined by "and" are plural, so the pronoun must be "their hours."
n.1: The sentence shifts from third person ("a student") to second person ("you"); keep the same person throughout.
n.2: "All" refers to "incubators" (plural) here, so the pronoun must be plural: "their filters."

E.q: A nursing applicant is studying a list of commonly misspelled words before the TEAS. Which words are spelled correctly? Select all that apply.
o: embarass
occurrence
seperate
definately
privilege
accommodate
E.w: Accommodate (double c, double m), occurrence (double c, double r) and privilege (i-l-e-g-e) are correct.

n.0: The correct spelling is "embarrass", with double r and double s.
n.2: The correct spelling is "separate", with a after the p.
n.3: The correct spelling is "definitely", from the root finite.

E.q: Jamal is paraphrasing a point from page 47 of a 2022 journal article by Maria Rivera in Nursing Today. His instructor requires APA style. Which in-text citation is formatted correctly?
o: (Rivera 47)
(Rivera, p. 47)
(Nursing Today, 2022, p. 47)
E.w: APA is an author-date style: the author's last name, a comma and the year, with the page (p. 47) added when the citation points to a specific part of the source: (Rivera, 2022, p. 47).

n.1: Author and page number with no year and no comma is MLA's author-page format, used mainly in the humanities.
n.2: APA is an author-date style, so the year must follow the author's name; a citation with only the author and page is incomplete.
n.3: APA in-text citations name the author, not the journal; a title stands in only when a source has no author, and this article has one.

E.q: For a paper on sleep and memory, Gabriela restates one paragraph from a journal article in her own words and her own sentence structure, keeping it about the same length as the original. What has she written, and does it need a citation?
o: A paraphrase, and it needs no citation
A summary, and it needs a citation
A direct quotation, and it needs a citation
A paraphrase, and it needs a citation
E.w: A paraphrase restates a specific passage in the writer's own words and sentence structure at about the same length. Because the ideas still belong to the source, a paraphrase must be cited.

n.0: Changing the words does not make the ideas hers; a paraphrase without a citation is plagiarism.
n.1: A summary condenses the main ideas and is much shorter than the original; Gabriela kept the passage about the same length.
n.2: A direct quotation uses the source's exact words in quotation marks; Gabriela used her own words.

E.q: An editor is checking apostrophes in a community health newsletter. Which sentences use apostrophes correctly? Select all that apply.
o: The clinic changed it's phone number.
The children's clinic closes at five.
The Garcia's are moving to Denver.
Those coats are their's, not ours.
The Garcias' house is on Elm Street.
We'll review the patients' charts today.
E.w: Children's (irregular plural + 's), Garcias' (plural family name ending in s + apostrophe), and we'll and patients' (contraction and plural possessive) are all correct.

n.0: The possessive pronoun is "its"; "it's" means "it is" or "it has".
n.2: The family name is a plain plural here (the Garcias are moving), so it takes no apostrophe.
n.3: Possessive pronouns such as "theirs" take no apostrophe.

E.q: Read the sentence from a radiology department update: "The quality of the images from the older scanners have improved since the software update." Which revision corrects the agreement error?
o: Change "scanners" to "scanner."
Change "images" to "image."
Change "have improved" to "were improved."
Change "have improved" to "has improved."
E.w: The subject is "quality" (singular). "Of the images from the older scanners" is an intervening phrase, so the verb must be singular: "has improved."

n.0: "Scanners" is inside a prepositional phrase and is not the subject; the plural verb "have" would still disagree with "quality."
n.1: "Images" is also inside a prepositional phrase; the true subject "quality" still needs "has," so the error remains.
n.2: "Were" is still plural, so it does not agree with the singular subject "quality," and it changes the meaning to passive.

E.q: An X-ray of the patient's stiff knee showed arthritis, and the nurse practitioner discussed treatment options with him. Based on its suffix, what does arthritis mean?
o: Surgical repair of a joint
Pain in a joint
Inflammation of a joint
A tumor of a joint
E.w: arthr/o means joint and -itis means inflammation, so arthritis is inflammation of a joint.

n.0: Surgical repair is -plasty (arthroplasty), not -itis.
n.1: Joint pain is arthralgia; pain is -algia, not -itis.
n.3: A tumor or mass is -oma, not -itis.

E.q: Read the sentence from a hospital memo: "The council decided that the new policy would ensure that personnel were not allowed to leave there stations early." Which word is used incorrectly?
o: personnel
ensure
there
council
E.w: The stations belong to the personnel, so the possessive "their" is required: "leave their stations".

n.0: "Personnel" (staff) is correct; "personal" means private.
n.1: "Ensure" (make certain) is correct; "insure" means to buy insurance.
n.3: "Council" (a group that makes decisions) is correct; "counsel" means advice.

E.q: A patient is writing about a clinic visit for a hospital blog that follows US conventions. Which sentence punctuates the quotation correctly?
o: The nurse said, "Take this with food," and handed me the cup.
The nurse said, "take this with food," and handed me the cup.
The nurse said, "Take this with food", and handed me the cup.
The nurse said "Take this with food," and handed me the cup.
E.w: In US style, a comma separates the dialogue tag from the quotation, the quoted sentence begins with a capital letter, and the comma after the quotation goes inside the closing quotation mark.

n.1: A quoted full sentence begins with a capital letter: "Take".
n.2: US style places commas inside the closing quotation mark, not outside.
n.3: A comma is needed after "said" to introduce the quotation.

E.q: Read the sentence from a staff policy: "Staff should utilize the aforementioned procedure in order to facilitate patient egress." Which revision replaces the inflated wording with plain language and keeps the meaning?
o: Staff should use the procedure described above as needed.
Staff should use this procedure to help patients leave.
Staff should employ the stated procedure to facilitate patient egress.
Staff should use the aforementioned procedure to help patients leave.
E.w: Plain language replaces inflated words: utilize = use, facilitate = help, egress = leaving, in order to = to.

n.0: This version drops the purpose (helping patients leave), so it loses meaning.
n.2: "Employ," "facilitate" and "egress" are still inflated words for "use," "help" and "leave."
n.3: "Aforementioned" is still an inflated word; plain language would say "this procedure."

E.q: Before the clinical trial began, researchers sorted the volunteers into groups so that each group was homogeneous in age. Based on its prefix, what does homogeneous mean here?
o: Different throughout
Many in number
Divided into halves
Similar throughout
E.w: homo-/homeo- means same or similar, so a group homogeneous in age is made of people of similar ages.

n.0: Different is hetero- (heterogeneous), the opposite prefix.
n.1: Many is multi- or poly-, not homo-.
n.2: Half is hemi- or semi-, not homo-.

E.q: A nurse is documenting what a worried parent asked at the bedside. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
o: Mrs. Diaz asked, "Is my son's surgery finished?".
Mrs. Diaz asked, "Is my son's surgery finished?"
Mrs. Diaz asked "is my son's surgery finished?"
Mrs. Diaz asked, "Is my son's surgery finished"?
E.w: The quoted words are a question, so the question mark belongs inside the closing quotation mark, and it also ends the sentence; no second end mark is added.

n.0: The question mark already ends the sentence; adding a period doubles the end punctuation.
n.2: A comma should introduce the quotation, and the quoted sentence should begin with a capital letter.
n.3: The question mark belongs to the quotation, so it goes inside the closing quotation mark.

E.q: Lucia is writing a personal statement for a nursing program's admissions committee. Which sentences are appropriate for this audience and purpose? Select all that apply.
o: My long-term goal is to work as a pediatric nurse in a rural clinic.
Nursing has been my dream for years, and I am super excited to start!
Without a doubt, I will be the strongest student your program has admitted.
Caring for my grandmother after her stroke showed me what skilled nursing looks like.
Volunteering at a hospice taught me to listen before I act.
E.w: A personal statement may use first person, but it must stay formal and purposeful. The correct sentences give specific experiences and goals in standard language.

n.1: The intensifier "super" and the exclamation point are too casual for an admissions committee, and the sentence gives no specific experience.
n.2: The boastful, unsupported claim is arrogant and does not suit a formal personal statement.

E.q: A unit manager is editing a weekly staffing update. Which of the following sentences is structured correctly?
o: The clinic was short-staffed on Friday. Because several walk-ins arrived before nine.
The clinic was short-staffed on Friday several walk-in patients arrived before nine.
Although the clinic was short-staffed, the nurses kept every visit on schedule.
The clinic was short-staffed on Friday, several walk-in patients arrived before nine.
E.w: A dependent clause (Although the clinic was short-staffed) followed by a comma and an independent clause is a correct complex sentence.

n.0: The second word group begins with "Because" and has no independent clause, so it is a fragment.
n.1: Two independent clauses with no punctuation or conjunction form a run-on (fused) sentence.
n.3: Two independent clauses joined by only a comma form a comma splice.

E.q: A board member's comment is quoted in a hospital newsletter. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
o: She called the plan "a good start;" the board disagreed.
She called the plan, "a good start"; the board disagreed.
She called the plan "a good start," the board disagreed.
She called the plan "a good start"; the board disagreed.
E.w: In US style, semicolons and colons go outside the closing quotation mark (only periods and commas go inside).

n.0: A semicolon goes outside the closing quotation mark.
n.1: The quoted words are part of the sentence's structure (the plan is called something), so no comma should introduce them.
n.2: A comma alone between two independent clauses creates a comma splice.

E.q: As Owen drafts an essay on hospital volunteering, a classmate tells him to stop and look up the spelling of each unfamiliar word as soon as he types it. Based on the writing process, what is the best advice for Owen?
o: Keep drafting, and check the spelling later during editing
Keep drafting, and check the spelling later during revising
Keep drafting, and leave the spelling for the publishing stage
Stop drafting, since spelling must be fixed before revising
E.w: Drafting focuses on getting ideas down in sentences and paragraphs, not on perfection. Spelling is a sentence-level correction handled during editing (and the final proofread), which comes after revising and before publishing.

n.1: Revising deals with content and organization (adding, moving and cutting material); spelling is a sentence-level fix that belongs to editing.
n.2: Publishing is submitting or sharing the final copy; spelling must already be corrected by then, during editing and the final proofread.
n.3: Spelling is checked during editing, which comes after revising, not before it; stopping to fix each word while drafting interrupts the flow of ideas.

E.q: A student is writing a paragraph organized from the least to the most important point. Place the sentences in the order that creates the most logical paragraph, starting with the first sentence.
o: One benefit is simple: the rent and utility bills are split in half.
A roommate in the same program can also quiz you before major exams.
Most important, a roommate who knows long clinical days offers support when the work feels overwhelming.
Sharing an apartment with a classmate during nursing school has real advantages.
E.w: The topic sentence comes first. "One benefit" opens the list, "also" adds a second point, and "Most important" signals the final, strongest point in order-of-importance organization.

E.q: A writing tutor reviews sentences from nursing students' reflection papers. Which sentences use irregular verbs correctly? Select all that apply.
o: The pipes in the old wing had froze before the heat came back on.
The intern has chose a specialty in pediatric nursing.
Ms. Reyes has led the infection control team since 2021.
The patient has already swum two laps in the therapy pool.
The phone rung three times before anyone at the desk answered.
By noon, the volunteers had drunk all of the bottled water.
E.w: Drink, drank, drunk; lead, led, led; swim, swam, swum. Each helping verb (had, has) is paired with the correct past participle.

n.0: After "had," use the past participle "frozen": "had frozen."
n.1: After "has," use the past participle "chosen": "has chosen."
n.4: The simple past of "ring" is "rang"; "rung" is the past participle and needs a helping verb.

E.q: Read the sentence: "Whenever the alarm sounds, the staff report to the lobby." Which part of the sentence is the independent clause?
o: Whenever the alarm sounds, the staff
the staff report to the lobby
Whenever the alarm sounds
to the lobby
E.w: "The staff report to the lobby" has a subject (staff) and a verb (report) and can stand alone as a sentence.

n.0: This joins the dependent clause to the subject but leaves out the verb, so it is not a clause.
n.2: "Whenever" is a subordinating conjunction, so this clause is dependent.
n.3: "To the lobby" is a prepositional phrase with no subject or verb.

E.q: The pharmacist reassured the patient that the drug's side effects are reversible once the medication is stopped. Based on its root, what does reversible mean?
o: Able to be sent back
Able to be pulled back
Able to be turned back
Able to be built again
E.w: re- means back or again, the root vers means turn, and -ible means able to be, so reversible means able to be turned back (undone).

n.0: Sending is the meaning of mit/mis (as in remission or transmit), not vers.
n.1: Pulling is the meaning of tract (as in retract), not vers.
n.3: Building is the meaning of struct (as in reconstruct).

E.q: Read the paragraph from a hand-hygiene poster. (1) Hand hygiene prevents infection. (2) Staff should wash for at least twenty seconds they should also dry their hands fully. (3) Sanitizer works when hands are not visibly soiled. (4) Gloves do not replace washing. Which sentence is a run-on?
o: Sentence 1
Sentence 2
Sentence 3
Sentence 4
E.w: Sentence 2 runs two independent clauses (Staff should wash ...; they should also dry ...) together with no punctuation or conjunction.

n.0: Sentence 1 is a single independent clause.
n.2: Sentence 3 is a complex sentence: an independent clause plus the dependent clause "when hands are not visibly soiled".
n.3: Sentence 4 is a single independent clause.

E.q: A nurse is writing an incident note about several patients who share a room on a pediatric unit. Which sentence uses plural and possessive forms correctly?
o: The patients' in Room 4 asked about the children's toys.
The patients in Room 4 asked about the children's toys.
The patients in Room 4 asked about the childrens' toys.
The patient's in Room 4 asked about the children's toys.
E.w: "Patients" is a plain plural subject, so it takes no apostrophe. "Children" is an irregular plural that does not end in s, so its possessive adds 's: "children's".

n.0: The patients do not own anything here, so "patients'" (plural possessive) is wrong; the plain plural is needed.
n.2: "Children" already is plural; an irregular plural not ending in s takes 's, so "childrens'" is wrong.
n.3: "Patient's" uses an apostrophe to make a plain plural; plurals that show no ownership take no apostrophe.

E.q: Which statement could a student include in a health science paper without a citation because it counts as common knowledge?
o: Researcher Dana Kim's finding that 38% of new nurses leave within two years
A hospital report's estimate of the average cost of each patient fall
Dr. Omar Hale's argument that nurses need longer breaks during shifts
The fact that the heart pumps blood through the body's blood vessels
E.w: Common knowledge is widely known, undisputed information that readers could find in many general sources, such as the heart pumping blood. It does not need a citation.

n.0: A specific statistic from one researcher's study is that researcher's finding and must be cited.
n.1: A cost estimate from a particular report is specific data from a source and must be cited.
n.2: An argument made by a named expert is that person's idea, so using it requires a citation even if it is paraphrased.

E.q: After routine blood work showed a decline in organ function, the patient's primary care provider referred him to a nephrologist. Based on its root, which organs does a nephrologist specialize in?
o: The liver
The nerves
The kidneys
The lungs
E.w: nephr/o means kidney and -logist means specialist, so a nephrologist specializes in the kidneys.

n.0: The liver is hepat/o (hepatologist).
n.1: Nerves are neur/o, the look-alike root (neurologist).
n.3: The lungs are pneum/o or pulmon/o (pulmonologist).

E.q: A volunteer coordinator is writing a note about visitors in the hospital lobby. Which sentence uses "their," "there," and "they're" correctly?
o: Their leaving their coats over there by the door.
They're leaving there coats over there by the door.
They're leaving their coats over their by the door.
They're leaving their coats over there by the door.
E.w: "They're" is the contraction of "they are", "their" shows possession (their coats), and "there" names a place (over there).

n.0: The sentence needs "they are leaving", so the contraction "they're" is required, not the possessive "their".
n.1: The coats belong to them, so the possessive "their" is required, not the place word "there".
n.2: "Over ___" names a place, so "there" is required, not the possessive "their".

E.q: A student is writing a short narrative paragraph for a nursing school application. Place the sentences in the order that creates the most logical paragraph, starting with the first sentence.
o: Last summer, Elena decided to earn her nursing assistant certificate.
Two weeks later, she started her first job at a nursing home.
When the course ended, she passed the state skills exam on her first try.
During the course, she practiced skills such as bed baths and safe transfers.
She enrolled in a six-week evening course at the community college.
E.w: The paragraph is in chronological order: the decision, enrolling, practicing during the course, passing the exam when it ended, and starting a job two weeks later.

E.q: A nurse manager is writing a formal report to a hospital's board of directors: "The pilot program cut readmissions by 12 percent, which is a pretty big deal for a unit of our size." Which phrase should be revised?
o: the pilot program
a pretty big deal
cut readmissions
by 12 percent
E.w: "A pretty big deal" is slang. A formal report needs precise wording such as "a significant improvement for a unit of our size."

n.0: "The pilot program" is a precise, standard name for a trial program.
n.2: "Cut readmissions" is clear and accurate; "cut" is a standard verb for a reduction.
n.3: "By 12 percent" is a specific, formal way to report the result.

E.q: A new graduate is writing a cover letter about relocating for a nursing job. Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
o: After moving to the Midwest, she drove south to visit her family.
After moving to the midwest, she drove south to visit her family.
After moving to the midwest, she drove South to visit her family.
After moving to the Midwest, she drove South to visit her family.
E.w: A compass word is capitalized when it names a region (the Midwest) but not when it gives a direction (drove south).

n.1: "The Midwest" names a region of the country, so it is capitalized.
n.2: Both are reversed: the region is capitalized and the direction is lowercase.
n.3: "Drove south" gives a direction, not a region, so it is lowercase.

E.q: Read the sentence from a county health report: "The new program did a lot of good things for people in the area." Which revision replaces the vague words with specific ones?
o: The new program provided free flu shots to 2,300 county residents.
The new program did many helpful things for many people in the county.
The new program helped a large number of local people in several ways.
The new program was very beneficial in a number of important ways.
E.w: Precise writing replaces vague words (things, stuff, a lot) with specific facts: what was provided, to whom and how many.

n.1: "Many helpful things" is still vague; it does not say what the program did.
n.2: "A large number" and "several ways" are still vague; the sentence never says what was done or for how many.
n.3: "Beneficial in a number of important ways" sounds formal but gives no specific detail.

E.q: Read the paragraph: "Community gardens offer more than fresh vegetables. Neighbors who garden together get to know one another and share skills. Gardeners also get regular outdoor exercise, and families eat more produce when they help grow it." Which sentence best concludes the paragraph?
o: Some gardeners prefer raised beds because they are easier on the back and knees.
In short, a community garden builds both good health and neighborly ties.
Vegetables such as tomatoes and peppers need at least six hours of sun each day.
However, many cities now charge a yearly fee for each garden plot in the spring.
E.w: A concluding sentence sums up the main idea without adding new information. This one ties together the social, exercise and nutrition benefits.

n.0: This sentence adds a new, minor detail instead of wrapping up the main point.
n.2: This sentence adds a new gardening fact unrelated to the benefits the paragraph lists.
n.3: This sentence introduces a new idea (fees) that the paragraph has not developed.

E.q: Read the sentence from a shift report: "The charge nurse divided the six patients between Tomas and I so that each of us had three." Which revision corrects the pronoun error?
o: Change "had" to "have."
Change "I" to "me."
Change "us" to "we."
Change "I" to "myself."
E.w: "Between" is a preposition, so both of its objects take the objective case: "between Tomas and me."

n.0: "Each" is singular, so "had" (or "has") is right; "have" adds a tense shift and does not fix "between Tomas and I."
n.2: "Us" is correct as the object of the preposition "of"; "each of we" would create a new error.
n.3: "Myself" needs an antecedent in the sentence that refers to the same person; the object of "between" needs "me."

E.q: To plan an essay, Andre writes "sleep loss" in a circle in the center of a page, draws lines out to circles labeled "memory," "mood," and "driving," and then adds smaller circles branching from each. Which prewriting strategy is he using?
o: Clustering
Freewriting
Outlining
Listing
E.w: Clustering (also called mind mapping or webbing) puts the central topic in the middle of the page and branches related ideas out from it in linked circles.

n.1: Freewriting is writing continuous sentences for a set time; Andre is drawing linked circles, not writing prose.
n.2: Outlining arranges ideas in a labeled hierarchy (I., A., 1., a.) in lines of text, not in a web of circles around a center.
n.3: Listing jots ideas down in a vertical list; it does not connect ideas visually to a central topic.

E.q: During chemotherapy, a patient's blood test revealed leukopenia, so the nurse reviewed infection precautions with him. Based on its word parts, what does leukopenia mean?
o: A deficiency of white blood cells
A cancer of the white blood cells
An excess of white blood cells
A deficiency of red blood cells
E.w: leuk/o means white and -penia means deficiency, so leukopenia is a shortage of white blood cells (which explains the infection precautions).

n.1: Cancer would be shown by carcin/o or -oma (or -emia in leukemia, a blood condition); -penia means deficiency.
n.2: An excess would use hyper- or -cytosis; -penia means deficiency.
n.3: Red is erythr/o; leuk/o means white.

E.q: Read the sentence from a discharge summary: "After reviewing the lab results, a new medication was ordered." Which revision corrects the dangling modifier?
o: After reviewing the lab results, the doctor's decision was to order a new medication.
After reviewing the lab results, the doctor's order called for a new medication.
After reviewing the lab results, a new medication was ordered by the doctor.
After reviewing the lab results, the doctor ordered a new medication.
E.w: The person who reviewed the results (the doctor) must be the subject right after the introductory phrase.

n.0: The subject after the comma is "decision," and a decision cannot review lab results; "doctor's" is only a possessive.
n.1: The subject after the comma is "order," so the sentence says the order reviewed the results; the doctor must be the subject.
n.2: The subject after the comma is still "a new medication," so the sentence still says the medication reviewed the results.
